utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that there are no preliminaries; therefore, the witness can be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bowen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen and Mr. Jeremy, if you would develop a speed of speech as I have developed over the last two minutes, then you make life far easier for both our interpreters and for the transcribers. If that is understood, I hope that I don't have to remind you, but the proof of the pudding is in the eating. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Bowen.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to begin by making a clarification to the discussion that we were having at the very end of your testimony yesterday, and in particular in relation to the -- the departure of civilians from Cerska. Now, at transcript page 18055, lines 7 to 9, the transcript records me as asking you as follows: "Q. Did you have any idea about where those Bosnian Serb civilians who were in Cerska had gone?" You then proceeded to answer the question as follows: "A. The assumption was that they had fallen back towards Srebrenica." Now, I intended to ask you about Bosnian Muslim civilians leaving Cerska rather than Bosnian Serb civilians, but I wanted to clarify with you which population group were you referring to in your answer?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well -- yeah, well, I misheard your slip of the tongue, so I thought you were talking about Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that was what I my answer was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ms. Stewart will now play a video-clip related to the movement of civilians into Srebrenica, 65 ter 22510I.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: "Each attempt to evacuate civilians in Srebrenica so far has ended in chaos. Desperate people have rushed the UN lorries, some of the weakest have been killed in the crush. But the UNHCR it seems now believes it's found a better way to do it. It says it has 60 trucks on standby. The plan is take 20 into the town every day partially loaded with food. On their way out, they'll evacuate between 1.000 and 1500 people. The UNHCR hopes to rescue up to 15.000, a little less than half the population of the town. The UNHCR denies it's assisting in the Serb's policy of ethnic cleansing. "The people we are evacuating from Srebrenica have already been ethnically cleansed because they are coming from areas that have fallen under Serbian control. They are not people from Srebrenica. They are refugees arriving -- "From the villages -- "Villages around and also from Konjevic Polje, from Cerska, areas that were -- fall under Serbian control a couple of weeks ago. "The Serbs who surround Srebrenica and control who goes in and out seem to be stepping up their offensive in the area. Privately, aid workers believe that the fall of the town is only a matter of time and that the civilian population must be evacuated before that happens. The next 48 hours the UNHCR believes will be crucial."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd just like to verify whether transcription, et cetera, is complete, and whether everything was duly translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, a transcript for this particular clip was provided to the booths in advance and they verified it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, the speed of speech in the video was still very high. But if I hear no further messages that you need more time, then you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, did you recognise that report?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And do you recall the approximate date of the report?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's around -- it was around April, I think, April of 1993. Or was it 1994? It was the April after the fall of Cerska which we were discussing yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. The -- the man in the clip that we saw who -- who stated that the people being evacuated from Srebrenica had already been ethnically cleansed from elsewhere. Do you recall who that was?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a special envoy for the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, and his name was, I think, Jose Maria -- I can't remember his surname be to be honest with you. But he was is a very senior envoy for the UNHCR who -- even much more than a spokesman. He was someone who went into big meetings with leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And the pattern that he describes of persons in Srebrenica being persons who've been ethnically cleansed from areas around Srebrenica, is that the pattern of population displacement that you were referring to at the end of your testimony yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was referring to that sort of pattern where people would fall back towards what they regarded as the next safer area or more secure area for them, as the military pressure from the Bosnian Serb side continued on the places where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender that clip as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22501I receives number P2529, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2529 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, in paragraph 11 of your statement, P2515 MFI, you discuss your visit to Bijeljina in 1994, where you met a local Bosnian Serb official who you state was involved in "shipping out Muslims." I'd now like to show you a video in connection with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: 65 ter 22511C, and we're going to start it from 56 seconds. And, Your Honours, the transcript for this clip has been provided to the booths in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: "At his office, Vojkan had assembled some of the last Muslims left in his Bijeljina. He said they're his friends. Vojkan is president of the regional commission for the free movement of the civilian population. That means he's in charge of ethnic cleansing. A report prepared for the UN says he's led groups of armed men who have been terrorising the Muslim community. Vojkan cheerfully denies it all. "He's turned ethnic cleansing into an official procedure and turned Bijeljina into such an ethnically Serb town that these Muslims are desperate to get out. "When permission came through for them to leave, Vojkan made sure we were there. He gave them time to say their goodbyes and to pack up the few possessions that hadn't been stolen. Deportations are no longer done at gunpoint, but Serbs like Vojkan are no less determined to remove Muslims from their towns. It's still ethnic cleansing."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, the official that you refer to in paragraph 11 of your statement, is that the official we see here, Vojkan?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Ah, his name was Vojkan Jerkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And in the report you state that Vojkan had turned ethnic cleansing into "an official procedure." Can you explain that observation in a little more detail, please?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well -- well, as I hope you had an impression from that clip -- and we went into it in greater depth in the film. That was from a one-hour documentary I did about a journey through the so-called corridor going through right across the Serb-controlled areas. He -- it had become a bureaucratic procedure. These were people who, according to the testimony of the people concerned, and we showed a little bit of it from that -- that old man and the woman who were there in that clip, they were people who said they had been highly intimidated by the way that life was in Bijeljina by that particular time. Wholesale deportations at gunpoint had ceased, but the people who were left behind were steadily being squeezed out, and it had got to the point where there was a bureaucratic procedure involving forms and an office where it would happen. And Vojkan Jerkovic even said that his mission -- elsewhere in the piece he says that he -- he is expecting the Nobel Peace Prize for what he was doing to try to help community relations. So what they were doing, as you saw there, was there was an office and he would arrange the transportation and they would go. But they were thoroughly intimidated and it seems to me, and also to the United Nations report that actually prompted us to seek him out, that the consequences were the same, the trauma was similar; but instead of being pushed out at gunpoint or bayonet point, they were being pushed out by the changed realities on the ground, that the ethnic balance had been changed in the town, there were people of extreme views who were in charge, and they were working very hard to continue the process of pushing them out. And as they said in those clips, at night-time and away from TV cameras there was still intimidation that was forcing people out; their homes being taken, people being beaten up, break-ins and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender that clip as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document receives number P2530, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For me, granted leave to consult --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, the entire procedure is a bit too fast for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Mr. Mladic is expected to remain seated. Let's first deal with the decision on admission. P2530 is admitted into evidence. If you need time to briefly consult, Mr. Ivetic, you have an opportunity to do so. Mr. Jeremy, you're on your feet. It was unclear to me whether you wanted to intervene at this moment in what happened or not, not to say that you should not be on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Oh, I'll give Mr. Ivetic a little bit of time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, from Sarajevo you covered events in Srebrenica in July 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I was in Sarajevo at the time of the -- the fall of Srebrenica and it's takeover by Bosnian Serb forces, and we weren't able to travel from Sarajevo to Srebrenica so we did it from Sarajevo itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to show you the final video in connection with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: "The first pictures of the Srebrenica enclave since it fell were broadcast by Bosnian Serb TV this evening. The Dutch UN peacekeepers, who are effectively prisoners, could only watch as Bosnian Serb soldiers performed for the cameras, handing out chocolate. "General Ratko Mladic, Commander-In-Chief of the Bosnian Serb army, addressed the crowd. Don't be afraid, he said, buses will take you to Muslim territory. Women and children first. Nobody will hurt you. The crowd of women and old men chorused 'thank you' as he went about his business." "Today the business has been ethnic cleansing. Around 30.000 people, almost all of them Muslims, were trapped in the enclave. Tonight the picture showed no Bosnian men of fighting age. The UN says all males over 16 are being interviewed as suspected war criminals. "Successful action against Muslim terrorists continues, the headline said. Radovan Karadzic, leader of the Bosnian Serbs, was in the studio. This, he said, is the latest is a example of the superiority of the Serbian people. Threats from the international community mean nothing to us. If NATO attacks, we must defend. He said that if Muslims in Zepa and Gorazde, the other safe areas in Eastern Bosnia, don't give up their weapons, the Serbs must attack. And as for the people who are leaving Srebrenica, he said that nobody was forcing them to go. "Well, it's ethnic cleansing with a twist, I'd say. The difference is that first of all these people don't want to try out on their own backs the hospitality of the Bosnian Serb army. They have heard them. Many have felt that hospitality previous. Many of those people are refugees from other areas that have been ethnically cleansed by the Bosnian Serbs. "What has the UN got to say about ethnic cleansing? "Well, the UN has always strongly condemned ethnic cleansing as genocide."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, do you recall where you got the footage for this particular report from?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I recall putting that report together very vividly, as a matter of fact. We were we reported -- we were able, technically, in Sarajevo, to record Bosnian Serbian TV that was broadcast from Pale, and we sat in the TV station in Sarajevo watching the news on Bosnian Serb television, and I think that was where we got the majority of those pictures from. It's possible that some were recorded from other sources and perhaps put in -- in London to improve the technical quality of them. But essentially all the pictures came out of Pale TV, and we were able to watch them in Sarajevo and record them and then use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And the person we saw towards the end of the clip who said that the UN had always condemned ethnic cleansing as genocide, do you recall who that was?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was a man called Alexander Ivanko. He was a spokesman for the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Getting to my final question, Mr. Bowen. Today we've discussed -- today and yesterday we've discussed Bosnian Muslim refugees that you experienced during your time in Bosnia during 1992, 1993, 1994, and 1995. Refugees in Sarajevo, Gorazde, Travnik, Trnopolje, Cerska, and Bijeljina, among other places. Can you estimate how many refugees you personally came into contact with, both interviewed and also saw with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say that in the course of those -- those years in Bosnia, I probably spoke to hundreds of refugees on a one-to-one level, and I saw thousands of them. Literally thousands. People in improvised shelters. People walking down the roads, freshly deported from their homes. People arriving on buses. People crying in refugee centres. It was is a very -- it was one of the constant themes of the war, that there were these refugees very often in a very poor and traumatised condition. And as I say, I spoke to very, very many of them, definitely in the hundreds, the high hundreds probably, and I saw certainly in the thousands, and that was just my own individual experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And of those refugees you've just referred to, what were your personal observations of the impact that this ethnic cleansing had had on those individuals and their families?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The impact of ethnic cleansing, of being ethnically cleansed, on those people was absolutely catastrophic. There is no question about that. In my experience as a journalist before that, which was already quite considerable, and since then, which is 20 years more experience, I've been to something like 17 or 18 wars now, and I've seen many, many refugees crises, and being a refugee is always traumatizing, but I think the way in which those ethnically cleansed people were displaced was particularly traumatic. It had a catastrophic effect on their lives. Often being deported at gunpoint at very short notice, sometimes with only minutes to get out of their house, grabbing almost nothing, being rendered homeless and penniless in a very short time. Quite often they would say -- and one of the things about dealing with these refugees was their stories were -- I heard the same stories again and again and again, over a period of years, and they said that very often they were kicked out by people they knew. They were kicked out as well violently, particularly in the early years of the war. The impact on them was absolutely catastrophic and traumatizing. I would generally be talking to either old men or to women, because the men of fighting age - this was again a characteristic - men of fighting age would be separated out and taken away. And quite often, some of those women and old men saw husbands or sons or brothers actually shot down in front of their eyes. I heard that repeatedly in Travnik with people who had come from Prijedor. And so they would sometimes as well talk about young teenage boys, 13 or 14-year-olds, who were also taken away with the older men. Now, for those people who came from villages, especially who came from quite traditional patriarchal societies, they were often quite literally left rudderless because, while the women a had a strong role in their communities, they were quite used to decisions being taken by the men. And the men would be taken away and these people would be cast off in this sea of trauma and loneliness and despair and fear and it was something which actually has stayed with me for the 20 years or so since then, seeing those people who were uprooted in such a brutal manner from where they lived, and it was absolutely horrific. And actually as a journalist, as the years went by, it became harder to get this on the air because there was almost an element of refugee fatigue among our news editors because of the fact that the stories were always the same. They were always very, very similar, and sometimes people would say: Are you talking again about these refugees who are again talking about being physically forced out of where they live. We've heard all this before, many, many times. And I think that -- and I would argue that that -- and I argued then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I'll go more slowly. I'll try to go more slowly. I argued then that the very fact that the stories were being repeated time and time and time again was a reason -- was what made them significant, even more significant because it was a pattern that emerged very early on in the war and it continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bowen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I've no further questions, Your Honours. There are two exhibits that I've used that I would like to tender. Firstly, the last clip that we viewed, 22879H.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection to 22879H.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22879H receives number P2531, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2531 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The second document is the document that I finished yesterday's session using, 65 ter 01027. That's the letter from the EC Monitoring Mission to General Mladic, dated 2 March 1993. This isn't a document that Mr. Bowen saw contemporaneously. His evidence does substantially overlap with the content of that document. Therefore, on that basis, I would tender it from the bar table now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We would object to that document as again it is one that was neither authored nor contemporaneously seen by the witness. His testimony yesterday could not corroborate the communications said to be contained therein. If the Prosecution wishes to bar table it, we would expect them to make a bar table submission with all the appropriate criteria as has been the case with the several bar table motions that have been filed, and we would then reserve further response based upon that submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a short document. It is a short document and where rules apply for bar table motions not directly in relation with specific witnesses, the Chamber has accepted and has explained why it accepted a single bar-tabled documents directly connected to the subject matter on which a witness testified. Therefore, the objection is denied. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 01027 receives number P2532, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2532 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Bowen.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, before we begin with my questions, I'd like to kindly ask you to try to ensure a pause between my question and your answer so that the court reporters and translators can do their work, and I will try to do the same after your answers. Is that understood, sir?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, first I want to make sure that I have your background accurately understood. Looking at the first page of your Rule 92 ter statement, which is P2515, marked for identification, you have a total of three languages listed, none of which are Serbo-Croatian. Can we conclude from the same that you are not fluent nor conversant in the Serbo-Croat language?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. As time went by in the Balkans, I picked a bit of it up, enough to speak a bit at roadblocks. But no, in no sense of the word am I fluent or conversant in the Serbo-Croat language.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was anyone from the BBC involved in vetting you for your testimony here today or for either your Rule 92 ter statement interview or the testimony in the Karadzic case which is also submitted under Rule 92 ter?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: By Rule 92 ter statement, you mean the witness statement that I made?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody from the BBC vetted me for my testimony or for my statement, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now first a general question for you, sir. Would you agree with me that a journalist has a professional obligation to accurately report facts of which they have knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you also agree with me that a journalist has a professional obligation to be impartial in the reporting of facts of which he has knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that a journalist has a professional obligation to investigate and verify facts given by others before reporting the same to ensure that they are accurate?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree up to a point. But sometimes it's necessary to report people's views, not to treat them as statements of fact but to make clear in one's reporting that you're reporting someone's view, someone's perception of a situation. So that doesn't mean that one would conduct a major investigation into, say, a statement made by somebody at a press conference or in an interview, particularly if that person was speaking from a position of responsibility. What you'd say is that this is the point of view given by that individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you feel that in the course of your reporting about the former Yugoslavia, you managed to maintain your obligation to be accurate and impartial?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now how about this witness statement that we have before us, P2515 marked for identification, do you believe that it too is true to the journalistic obligation to be accurate and impartial?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is true to that journalistic obligation and also to the statement that I made in front of the Court, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now is it correct that you had occasion to rely upon reports of amateur ham radio operators in Sarajevo for some of your information that you reported on for the BBC?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On a few occasions, we quoted and sometimes filmed the ham radio reports who were in touch from Sarajevo with some of the Bosnian government-controlled enclaves in Eastern Bosnia. "Rely," I think, would be too strong a word. We would quote them as one of the sources of information in the same way that I would quote, for example, the UNHCR or Bosnian Serb TV in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In those instances where you would quote amateur ham radio operators as sources, would you take any steps to verify such information before broadcasting the same?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the kind -- I think the way that I approached it would be to say information coming from those places is scarce. One of the ways in which people in Sarajevo get their information is via amateur ham radio operators. Now, I think it's important when you quote information like that to put the context in that, clearly, those ham radio operators were operating under their own particular set of circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of concerns during the time-period of others as to the accuracy or inaccuracy of ham radio reports?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a journalist, no matter what the story and no matter who speaks, I am always concerned about the accuracy of what they say because I am aware -- I was aware then, 20 years ago, and I am equally aware now, that people speak from their own perspectives always. People don't -- people are not objective. People speak through a subjective prism based on their own circumstances, education, and background. That's -- that's an absolute given, I think, in human communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 3 of the witness statement that we have in e-court, and it's page 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I want to look at paragraph 2 of the same with you. Here you state that you reviewed your original statement and relied on video reports for the purposes of this statement. Now insofar as there are no actual videos explicitly identified or referenced in this statement, can you tell us if you reviewed each and every single one of the reports that you generated about the former Yugoslavia prior to giving this statement or just some selection of the same.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did many video reports in the years from former Yugoslavia, some of them were different versions of the same story, so I can't say that I looked at every one of them. But in the period before I made this witness statement in June of 2009, I'd also written a book which wasn't just about the former Yugoslavia but former Yugoslavia featured in it, so to write that book I had also -- I'd gone through a very large number of video reports, which I have myself at home copies of, and as well as that I went through my original notebooks and also went back and talked to some of the people who I had worked with to -- to jog my memory. So I think that I was -- yes, I think I was well prepared, as a matter of fact, in terms of all the background information that I needed. Clearly, over a long period, sometimes you need to refresh your memory. But, yeah, I looked at -- I would say I'm very familiar with all the reports that I've seen that have been presented here as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Returning to the text of your statement that is before us on the monitors, at paragraph 4 you describe yourself as "quite an experienced war reporter" by the time the war started in Yugoslavia. And in paragraph 3 you identify a variety of places you reported from. Would it be more accurate to say that you reported on approximately 60 countries involving a number of armed conflict situations between 1987 and the mid-1990s?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably right, I should think. I mean, I couldn't say 60 exactly but -- and, of course, that's probably about right. I couldn't say 60 exactly. And you'll remember, of course, at that time that new countries were emerging. But, yeah, I was very busy and I travelled almost constantly. And from 1989, when I went to my first war in El Salvador, I went to many armed conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For those approximately 60 different countries where you reported on armed conflict situations prior to the war in Yugoslavia, did you actually see combat in any of those prior war zones?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to make it clear, it wasn't 60 different countries and 60 different war zones. That 60 included some relatively peaceful stories. But, yes, I had been in places where I had been under direct fire before I was in former Yugoslavia. In El Salvador, I had been in Baghdad when it was being bombed by the Americans and by the British and others. In 1991, I had been in Afghanistan, by then, when the Soviets were leaving. In 1992, before I was in Sarajevo, I was in Kabul when the Mujahedin took over the city, which was some extremely violent fighting with a large number of casualties which I saw and moments of great peril. So, yes, I had had pretty extensive experience of being under fire with armed men in different places, in different circumstances, different wars, regular armies, insurgent groups, by the time I got to Bosnia in 1992, and then, of course, also before that I'd been in Croatia in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then perhaps that is what leads to my confusion. With this prior combat experience, combat reporting experience, how is it that you couldn't believe your eyes in 1991 in Croatia when, in paragraph 5, you say you saw a tank firing?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the next sentence in the statement says why. It struck me that nothing like that had happened in Europe since 1945. My amazement was that, as a European, I was seeing tanks firing in anger on my continent in western -- pretty much for the first time. Yes, there had been maybe Hungary 1956. Tanks had been used, I suppose. But in terms of that kind of war, suddenly I saw in some cases World War II era tanks as well as more modern T-54s and so on being used. And my amazement was not that a tank was firing, but my amazement was that a tank was firing in Europe and that villages were burning and bodies were lying in the streets, and that's something that as a European, I hadn't expected to see. My experience of wars had been in Asia. It had been in Central America. It hadn't been in my own backyard. That's what amazed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we can get back to focusing on your background. Before you became a reporter, is it correct that you never served in the armed forces of any country in any capacity?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never served in the armed forces. Before I became a reporter, I was a graduate student of international affairs in the United States of America.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is it correct, as part of your education, that you never underwent any military training or education?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I was never in the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Arising out of your work as a journalist, is it correct that you received an award at the Monte Carlo Film and TV Festival in 1994 for a documentary you produced called "Unfinished Business," relating to events in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It was about the siege of the mainly Muslim eastern side of Mostar in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Apart from that award, has your work relating to the former Yugoslavia resulted in any other awards or honours?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a long time ago now. I got a medal from the New York TV Festival, I believe, at about the same time for coverage of Mostar. I think that was about it on former Yugoslavia in terms of awards.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned generally a book that you published. Is it correct that the book is entitled: "War Stories"?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Have you published any other books that have dealt with the former Yugoslavia apart from the one section in that book that relates to the same?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, though I have mentioned I last year published a book about the Arab uprisings, and that starts off with a mention of the testimony I gave, in fact, in this court against Radovan Karadzic, which was at the same time as the Tunisian revolution. And I think I make a comparison between the legal pursuit of some Arab leaders and the legal pursuit of some leaders from the former Yugoslavia. But apart from that mention, no, the -- what I have written in books about -- what I have written in books about former Yugoslavia was in that book "War Stories."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I seek clarification of that answer. You said: "I gave in fact --" you are talking about the testimony you said you gave, in fact, in this court against Radovan Karadzic. Did you mean to say that you gave evidence against Radovan Karadzic or that you gave evidence in the case against Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apologies, Your Honours. I am not quite sure of the legal distinctions. But I've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the legal distinction is the following: Witnesses are expected not to testify against or in favour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of a person but are expected to testify on the basis of their truthful recollection of events and that may happen in a case against a person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. Well I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may be called by one of the parties. And if the Prosecution calls you, then it's reasonable to expect that the Prosecution thinks that you could give evidence in support of their case which is a case against a person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood, Your Honour. And apologies for my misunderstanding of legal terminology. I appeared as a witness against Radovan Karadzic, and I was called by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are still repeating that you were a witness against a person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. I appeared as a witness in the trial of Mr. Karadzic -- Dr. Karadzic, and I was -- yeah, I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that if you used those words, that you did not intend to say that your testimony was coloured by an adverse position --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- against an accused. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is -- yes, Your Honour, that is well understood, and I simply gave testimony based on my honest recollection of what I had experienced at the time, and I was called by the Prosecution side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's been clarified. Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I would like to return to the tank which you saw firing in 1991 in Croatia for which you couldn't believe what you were seeing. I note, sir, that the statement, which we still have before us, at paragraph 5, with the references to the burning Croatian village, seems to imply that the tank you are talking about is a Serb tank firing unmolested at the Croats. But in fact, sir, you are reporting on a fire fight between a Yugoslav tank and Croat forces including a Croat tank; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't see any implication in that, that it was a Serb tank firing indiscriminately into a Croat village. In fact, it was a Croat tank in an area that was -- where a fight had been going on and the village was on fire, but the tank that I saw was not firing into the village. It was firing, I think, in another direction. No, it was a -- we had accessed that part of the fight from Zagreb, so I must have been on the Croatian side of the lines. So it was a Croat tank, yeah. I did not intend to imply, and I don't think I did imply, in that section that it was a tank belonging to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where, Mr. Ivetic, from that paragraph, do you get the impression that the witness implied that it was a Serb tank?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that the witness implied. I said that I believe that the statement seems to imply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, it is the witnesses's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Agreed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So answer my first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In reading the statement, Your Honours, it seems that he's talking about actions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's why --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- I am asking you to show us where in that paragraph you get that impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I got that impression from reading the entirety of the statement, Your Honour, which is focused on actions of Serbs. And to have an ambiguity where they don't specify what tank is firing, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's look at what you said, sir. At page 23, lines 13, you said: "Now, sir, I would like to return to the tank which you saw firing in 1991 in Croatia for which you couldn't believe what you were seeing. I note, sir, that the statement, which we still have before us, at paragraph 5, with the references to the burning Croatian village, seems to imply that the tank you are talking about is a Serb tank firing unmolested at the Croats."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that's the impression that every single member of my team that read this statement had, Your Honour. So I believe I was perfectly proper in seeking clarification on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I understand that. I'm asking -- you are directing the attention of the witness to paragraph 5 --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- where you say this impression is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I'm asking you: Can you show us from paragraph 5 where that impression comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: From reading paragraph 5 in the context of the entire statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. Ivetic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Your Honour. I see we are at the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could I invite you not to hide behind members of the team. You, as cross-examining counsel, are responsible for what you put to a witness. We leave it to that. We take a break. Mr. Bowen, you will be escorted out of the courtroom by the usher. We take a break and resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to come in, the Chamber notices that the response by the Defence on the 39th 92 bis motion has been filed yesterday. However, we had not yet put on the record that an extension of time was granted. The extension of time was granted on the 4th of October and the extension granted was 14 days. The new dead-line at that time set at the 17th of October. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Yes. And that the Chamber had informed the parties accordingly. That, therefore, hereby is now put on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I just clarify one of the points I made in my -- one of my answers in the previous session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's okay with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was asked about if I had served in the armed forces and the answer - correct answer - which I gave was: No, I haven't. But I've -- just in the interests of full disclosure, I spent some time with the British army as a young man when I was about 18 as a -- what they called a potential officer, when I was contemplating joining the military, and spent some time with them in Aldershot, which is a big British military town. Get the -- you know, spending time with them and doing some of the things that they did. So I had had some connections with them. That's all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's appreciated. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can call up 1D1339 in e-court, which should be the book authored by the witness. And if we could please turn to page 2 in e-court, which is pages 126 through 127 of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to direct at the bottom of page 126 and the top of page 127, I think we can see here that we are again talking about the very same tank that is in paragraph 5 of your statement. You say it looks like a remake of Kelly's Heros and you half expected to see Telly Savalas. Now I'd like to focus at the second paragraph beginning at the middle of the page which is labeled 127, which reads as follows: "The local Croatians had raided a military museum and towed away a T-34 tank, the kind that the Red Army drove from Stalingrad to Berlin to defeat the Nazis. Its gun still worked and they had the right kind of shells. So they dug the World War II veteran into the embankment of the motorway of Brotherhood and Unity that linked Zagreb and Belgrade. Every now and then they fired it at the Serbs who were about a mile away. "A hospital in what had been a spa town was full of wounded men. In the basement, tended by doctors and relatively safe, were the Croatian wounded. In a ward on the ground floor, next to big windows, wounded Serb fighters were tied to their beds during a barrage. The windows had been blown in by the shelling and the men who lay on the beds had fresh nicks and cuts on their arms and faces from shrapnel and glass. The tortured faces from the thought that the next shell might come in through the roof. They might as well have been pinned out in the sun for the vultures." Now, first of all, sir, is this account from your book an accurate and truthful account of the facts that you witnessed at that time?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is this, in fact, the same tank that is referenced in paragraph 5 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to the T-34 that was dug into the embank?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you or did someone at the Office of the Prosecutor make a conscious decision to remove any mention of the tank in paragraph 5 being a Croatian tank?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could just add something, sir. If you see in the previous paragraph, again I'm talking -- I'm talking about the tank that was moving, and at no time in that do I say it was a Serb tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, one other thing that I did not see a reference to in your statement was any significant coverage of the city of Mostar. Would you agree with me that Mostar, rather than Sarajevo, was the most vicious theatre of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I felt, in 1993, when I was in the east side of the Mostar, that albeit it was a small enclave, a small area, that the level of violence I saw there, the level of fight -- of -- of suffering was -- was worse than in Sarajevo. Yeah, I thought so at the time. That's not to minimise what I saw in Sarajevo, but it -- Sarajevo was a bigger area and it -- and the crucial difference was that it was -- there was a better supplied relief effort into Sarajevo. But all told, the level of suffering was greater in Mostar because there was virtually -- at that time in 1993, there was almost no relief aid getting in there. I had to get in there by walking over the mountains with the Bosnian army. There no easy road in. It was really pretty much completely cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And would you agree that another difference between Mostar and Sarajevo which led to your conclusion that Mostar was the most vicious theater of the war and, in fact, more devastated, was the lack of a existing black market in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the -- the absence of relief supplies meant that there was very little to trade on a black market in Mostar. There was a bit of a black market. There were some people who had connections across the lines, not least with local Serbs to the -- the east of -- further east, and there were some people who had some connections. But it was -- as I said, it was a much smaller enclave, and it was more -- more militarised and organised. I would say it was more comparable with the situation in, say, Gorazde, or even in Dobrinje in Sarajevo, than it was in the main part of the Sarajevo itself where, as is well known, there was a very thriving black market.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that despite not having a thriving black market, despite being more isolated than Sarajevo, East Mostar, controlled by the Muslim side, was able to maintain a steady stream of weapons and supplies such that the ABiH forces in that part of the city even carried out an offensive and captured significant ground from the Croats?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had a kind of Ho Chi Min trail that ran from Jablanica into Mostar, and that's the route I took to get in there. And I went in with a train of pack horses that was carrying a large number of -- well, fair number of mortar shells and small arms ammunition, and that was 1993. And, yeah, they were -- they were organised militarily there. And the Croats relied more on their heavy guns to bombard the city than using foot soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that the ABiH forces that were supplied by this Ho Chi Minh trail that you described were able to undertake an offensive and capture significant territory from the Bosnian Croat forces before being ordered by Sarajevo to stop their offensive?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the precise details and I'm not sure if that happened at a time when I was there, but I certainly remember the people who were involved in their military operations telling me that they had captured -- they -- they had pushed out their perimeter. I certainly remember being told that. Whether -- I wasn't privy to whether or not they had been told to desist by the authorities in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now getting back to Sarajevo. Did you have any occasion to consider or any knowledge that in Sarajevo, with an existing black market and not as geographically isolated as Mostar, the ABiH forces were able to equip themselves even better with weapons and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992 they weren't well equipped. I saw people, fighters, for example, who were armed with hunting rifles, not with proper military-grade automatic weapons, Kalashnikovs and the like. As the war went on and especially after they built their tunnel, yes, they were better organised and they organised themselves militarily. There is no doubt about that. Yeah. They were -- they became more organised as the -- as the years went by. In 1992, it was pretty chaotic and they didn't have much. But by 1994, 1995, they had more.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can focus on Sarajevo for a moment, would you agree with me that one of the other differences in between Sarajevo and Mostar was the fact that in Mostar the ABiH forces were very unified, whereas in Sarajevo there were many armed factions, often hostile to one another?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd say that's an accurate picture of the way that things were. They were -- again, it -- a lot of it came down to size. But in Mostar, the BiH forces were much more cohesive than they were in Sarajevo where they were definitely -- at different times were warring factions. Particularly in the sort of 1994, 1993-1994 period, there were a lot of -- there were a number of different warring factions within the city of Sarajevo. "Warring factions" is too strong. Rival factions, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for the sake of clarity, these rival factions would have all been BiH Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not wholly Muslim, no. At all times in the city, there were people of mixed birth and there were also people who were ethnic Croats and ethnic Serbs. So not overwhelmingly Muslim -- sorry, not wholly Muslim, but the certainly the vast majority of their leaders that I was aware of were Muslim. And most of the -- yeah, sure, most of the men who carried guns probably as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can now take a look at 1D1348 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is a -- this is the transcript of your testimony in the Prlic proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 46 of the same in e-court, that ought to correlate to transcript page 12756 of the underlying transcript. And if we can focus from line 3 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will quote the question and answer for you, sir, and then have some follow-up questions. "Q. Mr. Bowen, you have mentioned sniping now when you talked about your experience in East Mostar and also in your written statement there are several mentioning of sniper activities. My question is if you have observed or if you have been aware of any sniping activities from East Mostar to the west. That means if the Bosnian Muslim forces did use the same sniper activities as a way of fighting, or it was mainly concentrated on sniping activities from the west side of Mostar. "THE WITNESS: I didn't see it happening but I assumed it would have been happening. I'd assumed that that was a tactic that they'd use. The Bosnian army -- the Bosnian authorities used the -- the Bosnian army used that tactic in Sarajevo. Sniping went both ways across the front lines in Sarajevo, and I had no reason to doubt that sniping went both ways across the front lines in Mostar as well." Sir, first of all, does this accurately depict your answer to this question?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt the transcript, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is the answer truthful such that you would so testify again the same way today?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now in relation to the sniping tactic that the Bosnian authorities used in Sarajevo, could you please clarify for us, because in the Prlic case, in the pages leading up to this, there was talk of sniping against civilians who tried to cross the boundary line. Is that the type of tactic that you are talking about here or something else?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, are you referring now to Sarajevo or to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, when I'm talking about sniping activity -- do you mean sniping activities coming from the Serb side or coming from the Bosnian side?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: From the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that -- I mean, there was plenty -- there was plenty of evidence that on the Bosnian side there were snipers who shot over the front lines and into Serb-controlled territory. I personally never went and filmed one of the guys doing that. But I know I had colleagues who did, and there was video -- in fact, I used once -- I think in one of the my pieces, filmed by somebody else, of a Bosnian sniper shooting into the -- the Serb side, yeah. And sniping came the other way as well. It was a big hazard for people inside Sarajevo. But it's absolutely the case that sniping went both ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Jeremy, is it part of the Prosecution's case that there was no sniping from the Muslim side into Bosnian held -- Serb-held territory?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No, it's not, Your Honours. And in fact, one of the associated exhibits for this witness is the video that Mr. Bowen just referred to of Bosnian Muslim sniping into Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I understood your line of questioning to establish that there was sniping the other way which seems to be a fact which is not in dispute. Therefore, I wonder whether we could try to focus on matters which are in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I may refer to my question, Your Honours, I thought I was rather clear. In referencing the Prlic case where this witness testified and where was there was talk of sniping at civilians who were trying to cross the boundary between East and West Mostar, and I asked if, when he referred to sniping tactics, he was talking about sniping at civilians trying to cross the boundary line or to something else, and now he's described that in fact that it was something else. So I was trying to clarify which sniping tactic he was talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I could add something, sir. I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- thank you. I do not know if they were also sniping at people trying to cross the boundary line, but my impression was that they would get themselves into positions where they could see targets moving on the other side, and they would then shoot at them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can have a look at 1D1347 in e-court and page 33 of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This will be a transcript from another case you testified in, sir, the Martinovic and Naletilic case. And this will, I believe, be a selection from your documentary film "Unfinished Business," starting at line 4. I would like to have you follow along and then I will have some questions in relation to what is recorded there. "Hodza, Goran's commander, used a mirror to point out the whereabouts of a Croat sniper. He was in the tower. Hodza didn't try to hide the way the Bosnian army treats its prisoners either. A Croatian prisoner of war appeared in the trench we just crossed. Prisoners dug the trenches and lay sandbags in the most exposed and dangerous positions on the front lines. When they are not working, they are imprisoned in a sweaty, badly ventilated cellar. We could film, but we weren't allowed to talk to any of them. "One prisoner was badly wounded. He was in considerable pain. A lot of the prisoners had been hurt. The injuries were caused, their guards said with some relish, by Croat fire on the front line. The prisoners were thin, but they looked no worse fed than many civilians in East Mostar. The guard said that they eat the same food. "Their captors know that the work they do on the front line - here they were exhuming bodies - contravenes the Geneva Conventions. As far as they're concerned, though, that's better than seeing their own people doing it. In this war, there is no middle way. There are victors and there are victims. The Bosnian soldiers know which they want to be. They dug up these bodies to use them as currency in a prisoner exchange." Now first of all, sir, is all this truthful as to what you had knowledge of or saw in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just first seek clarification. What we listened to, is that part of a text of a video or is that testimony of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is, I believe, the documentary "Unfinished Business" produced by the witness. He can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore the first thing we would have to establish is who speaks and not treat it as if these were answers given during the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That having been clarified now, perhaps you could frame your question in such a way that this becomes clear so that we know what the witness is responding to, either to his own testimony or to what was shown to him in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, are these your own words from the documentary "Unfinished Business"?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What you read out was the script that I wrote for that documentary, which was designed, obviously, to work with the pictures. That was a script -- those were words to be written over pictures. And that is a -- an extract of the script of the documentary that was played as part of the evidence, I believe, in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is this script that was part of the documentary truthful as to what you had knowledge of and what you saw in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now was this tactic or this treatment of prisoners something that you also eye-witnessed in Sarajevo; for instance, when you saw Caco's men forcing people with shovels to the front lines?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a little bit different in Sarajevo, because Caco and his people were picking on members of the public they regarded as slackers. They would go around cafes and they would find men who weren't in uniform and who weren't in any kind of armed formation, and they would drag them out and march them up to the front line and make them dig trenches. And I saw that myself with my own eyes, a group these people in civilian clothes, carrying spades, being marched by armed men up past the Bistrica barracks and further up and up the hill, up that way, towards the front line, and that was a tactic that Caco used quite a bit. And among the people who supported him, it was a popular tactic. But those weren't -- as far as I'm aware, they weren't imprisoned fighters as they had been in Mostar. They were various civilians, and I've no knowledge of their ethnicities, who Caco and his people felt were not doing all they could during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we could return to your statement, P2515 marked for identification. At page 13 of the English, page 17 in the B/C/S. I'd like to focus on the last three lines of paragraph 42, where it is written: "Foreigners were less welcome. Some parts of Sarajevo were on the way to becoming effectively no-go areas for foreign reporters because of the hostility of local warlords." Was one of the local warlords that you identify here the person we've been talking about known as Caco, C-a-c-o, with the full name of Muslan Topalovic, commander of the ABiH unit known as the 10th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was specifically referring to Caco and the area of Sarajevo controlled by the 10th Mountain Brigade. I did actually -- if I could just add. I did manage to go to that area more than once because I knew people who lived there, but I never went with my camera or cameraman, or my flak jacket, or anything that would identify me as a journalist. That's how I managed to see his prisoners, for example, being marched up to the front line because I was just walking around with a friend of mine who was actually in the 10th Mountain Brigade. And so under the -- effectively the protection of this person, I was able to observe what was going on in there. But I absolutely couldn't film it. It would have been -- the camera would have been taken from me, at the very least.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you could please clarify for me, sir. A few moments ago you told me the activities of Caco did not involve prisoners. And now in answer to a different question, you say at line 14, "that's how I managed to see his prisoners."

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I was referring to the people inside Sarajevo who he had taken prisoner. They were his prisoners, his men's prisoners. They weren't what I suppose you would call prisoners of war, as far as I could tell. In other words, Serb combatants who had been captured. They were people, as I said, who were -- who had been picked up mainly in cafes and marched off to the front line. So they were prisoners, but they weren't prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Is it correct that the 10th Mountain Brigade led by this individual Caco had a fair number of foreign Mujahedin fighters in their midst?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard anything about that while I was in Sarajevo and I never saw anything. I never saw any foreign fighters who were part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could I seek clarification of one answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Earlier you told us in the examination-in-chief that you would try to get -- to enter Grbavica, and you managed I think only once in all those years. Do I understand this, paragraph 42, to say that whereas the Serb territory which was a no-go without permission, which you almost never got, that it now, within the city, in the Muslim-controlled areas, that similar situation slowly developed, that there were no-go areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it really wasn't quite the same thing, I would say, because to get to Dobrinja, you had to cross the front line, you had to cross the airport, which was effectively the front line, go to Lukavica barracks, get permission to go to Pale. In Pale get permission to go to Grbavica. And as I say, it happened to me one time only between 1992 and 1995, despite many, many requests. To get to the areas -- I said effectively no-go areas because what I meant by that was you could drive freely into them. You could get into your vehicle and drive from where we were based at the TV station to the area which was just past the Bistrica barracks where the -- the area that I understood to be the place that was controlled by, in that period, the 10th Mountain Brigade, and you could go into it, but if you then took out your camera, started working, they were hostile. And there were plenty of cases of people being arrested, their flak jackets being confiscated, their camera equipment being confiscated. So I never personally ever risked doing that because I never wanted to lose our flak jackets, our vehicle, or our camera equipment. But as I said, I managed to get into there and look around through my friend who was in the 10th Mountain Brigade. I didn't -- so effectively a no-go area in that you couldn't work there, but not nearly the same thing as crossing the front line and having to get permission to even go towards the territory. I could walk in without showing any papers, into that particular area, and look at what was happening, but what I couldn't do was take out a camera. It was effectively a no-go area, I suppose you would say, for a working foreign reporter working -- not working covertly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to Caco and his men, his unit, would you agree with they that undertook violent and undisciplined and even criminal actions in Sarajevo against both Serbs and non-Serbs alike?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I first heard about Caco, he had, I suppose, what we describe in Britain as a Robin Hood reputation because he -- when people were suffering from lack food, they had enough so they wouldn't starve because of the UNHCR's relief operation, but it was a very repetitive diet and no one was getting fat on it. So he broke open some government food stores and distributed the food to the poor and to the refugees and so on, and that made him for a while very popular. He became less popular when he appeared to be -- become getting out of control, and there were plenty of reports at the time of Caco intimidating Serbs, defying the government. He was also -- at the same time, his forces were carrying out military operations up on the front line. I know this from -- again from my friend and connection, who actually took part in some of them and who described to me how -- and it was a sign of the differences between the government and Caco, that this person was saying to me that they were doing their operation and the plan was that they would get some support from a government-controlled unit, which then didn't -- the support never arrived, and they lost fighters as a result of that. And those kinds of incidents made the -- the differences between the government and between Caco sharper.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, yesterday, the Prosecution started your examination by showing a video in relation to the Europa hotel in which we could see several men in civilian clothing walking around the hotel carrying Kalashnikov-type rifles and other weapons. You testified at transcript page 18035 that these men were various fighters who came in to help refugees. Are you really trying to tell us that these armed men carrying rifles were helping the evacuation rather than being stationed at the Europa hotel?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were helping the evacuation. I never saw -- and I visited the Europa hotel a lot. I never saw armed men stationed at the hotel. But there were in different places, at check-points and so on, in the city there were armed men, and on that particular day they -- that particular night, my clear understanding was that they'd come in to help evacuate some of the civilians who were -- some of whom were old and infirm, who were trying to get out -- and children as well, who were trying to get out of this burning building. At no time in the war, and as I say, I was a regular visitor to the hotel, I never saw armed men inside it stationed there, as a military headquarters or even as a place where they'd go to drink coffee in between shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that many of your visits to the Europa hotel were, in fact, to visit your friend who was a member of Caco's unit?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My friend and my friend's family, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we could --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, if I just could add something. After my friend joined Caco's unit, I saw more and more of the family and less and less of my friend, because my friend was not there. So actually I saw the mother, the sisters, and gave them coffee. And we had a lot of -- we brought provisions in with us, and I felt it was very unfair that we had so much and they had so little, so I did my bit to try and give a few things away.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one question in that respect. You say you visited Caco and his family in Hotel Europa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not Caco, I visited --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, no, your friend who was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- who was -- who -- who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- ultimately became a fighter in Caco's unit. But initially --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- was not, was just a regular civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just misspoke.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Why was your friend and his family living or stationed in the Hotel Europa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was her family. Because they were displaced from their homes which were right up -- very high up on the front line effectively, near the bobsleigh run.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could look at 1D1339 in e-court, and page 8 of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, sir, this is your book, and to be fair and to give the full picture, I'd like to focus on the bottom of the right-hand page, 139, where you talk about your friend and the Europa hotel. "Every few months after that, when I was in Sarajevo, I went to the Europa to try to find her. I usually gave her family a sack of provisions looted from the BBC stores. Often she wasn't there, and I left the food with her mother. The war was changing everything for civilians in Sarajevo. As it went on, they started to forget the lives they used to have and the dreams they had about the future. As peace recedes into the past, war takes over and crushes everything. My friend, and I think I shouldn't use her name, went back to her family home to look after her father. It was dangerous, but so was sitting around the squalid, burnt-out corridors of the Europa hotel. At least she was doing something, and soon she was doing more. She joined her father's army unit as a medic. I did not see her again until the following year, in Sarajevo Old Town near the Europa hotel. The black rings under her eyes were deeper and darker and she was wearing combat fatigues. She said she had become a fighter, and she told a story of deceit and failure." First of all, sir, is this selection from your book accurate and truthful as to the facts that are set forth therein?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is this the friend you've been talking about and, in fact, the story of deceit and failure the story that you told us a few moments ago about the offensive by Caco's men and the ABiH where the support did not arrive?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the incidents. Yeah, they were becoming -- the people who supported him were becoming progressively more alienated from the leadership of the Bosnian Serb -- sorry, the Bosnian government and its armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 11 of this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which should correlate to pages 144 and 145 of your actual book. And in -- on the left-hand side, the first full paragraph that starts out, "In Caco's domain," talks about one of the incidents we've talked about with the men who were -- who were being -- who were being sent to dig trenches. I'd like to pick up at the middle of that paragraph with something that I would like to ask you about, and it reads as follows: "After the war, some of Caco's men were also imprisoned for shooting Serb civilians for no reason other than their ethnicity. They threw the bodies of their victims into a ravine. My friend, who found herself in a world of violence, looked close to breaking, exhausted and pale. She was carrying a loaf of bread that she said was for her mother and sister. A man in her unit who protected her had been killed. She was not sure what was coming next." Is this also an accurate and truthful account of the activities -- of the facts that are set forth therein?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could return to P2515 marked for identification, which is again your witness statement, and look at page 7 in English and page 9 in the B/C/S, and I'd like to look at paragraph number 20 with you. You say: "Access to the city was always difficult. The reason was that the Bosnian Serbs decided who came in and who went out." And I want to ask you, did you consider that the actions of Caco and his men, and others like them, perhaps affected the ability of persons to leave Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fundamental reason why people couldn't leave the city was the siege. As time went by, there were people like Caco. But it would be wrong to say that they controlled large areas of the city or dominated its life. They were factors within it at different times. But the -- the fundamental unifying reason why people were not able to get out of the city, in my opinion, and based on my observations and evidence, was the siege with which the Bosnian Serbs invested the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We've already established that the -- at least one paragraph in your statement was a reference to Caco although it did not name him. Why was there no specific reference or identification of Caco in the paragraph of your statement that dealt with the activities that you were describing of him and his men?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we go back and look at that statement -- that paragraph again so that I know precisely what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. If we could look at page 13 in the English, page 17 in the B/C/S. That's -- the last part of the paragraph 42 was where we started the discussion as to Caco.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I wasn't -- I didn't mention his name there because at that particular point I wasn't getting into his whole story.
