I suppose it's my -- my instinct as a journalist that by raising a question about somebody, you then need to go into more detail as to who they are. But to simply say "local warlords," that probably said enough at that particular time. In no sense was I trying to gloss over what Caco had been doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that Caco was not the only such local warlord on the BiH side that you had knowledge of operating in this fashion?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right from the -- right from the beginning of the war, there were other strongmen, warlords if you like, who operated in Sarajevo and had a following of their own that was effectively independent of the -- what you might call the central authorities there. There were a couple of Celos, one of whom I got to know a little bit. There was Juka. There were -- yeah, there were people who were very well reported on at the time, who had these nicknames and were seen as semi-independent actors within the constellation of military forces there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could I ask one question to clarify. Did you gain any impression as to the quantitative aspect of that? Was it 30 per cent which were following warlords and having their own programme, not necessarily excluded from taking part in hostilities as well? Or was it 10 per cent or 70? Did you gain any impression about the importance of that -- those factions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the very beginning of the war, this guy -- and it was actually the months -- by the time I got there in July 1992, this guy, Juka, his star was already waning, but to start with he was a very prominent fighter who had organised a force. My impression was that these people were very much minority players. The one that was seen as the biggest potential threat by the government of President Izetbegovic was Caco, I'd say. And in the end they took action against him. But especially as the time went by and the Bosnian -- the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina became more organised, these people became less relevant. And it was the fact, though, that as the siege went on, the levels of crime increased, levels of corruption, black marketeering, and some of these people were -- most of these people became -- either were or became criminal or semi-criminal in their activities. And it was quite hard to -- sometimes to see where their supposed military activities ended and the criminal activities started. I remember one of the Celos, for example, at the beginning of the war he was like a mobster basically. But he also had been an effective fighter. He had a following and he had some tough guys who followed him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said they developed to be minority players --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, 49 per cent is minority --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and 5 per cent is minority. Is there --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Closer to 5 than 49. I am reluctant to get into numbers because I never knew exactly how many forces people had, but they were very much minority players, individuals with a small following, in the single figures, I would say, in terms of percentages, and not mass movements in any sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn back to 1D1339, page 9 in e-court, which should correlate to pages 140 to 141 of your book.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We've already talked about Juka Prazina, who is referenced at the bottom of page 140. I'd like to focus on the top of page 141, on the right-hand side, which I believe is the man that you've just talked about. So if you could follow with me, sir. "Fortunes were made trading food and cigarettes on the black market, which were smuggled into Sarajevo through the front lines and by corrupt UN soldiers and workers. The local mobsters became very powerful. I knew one of them slightly. He was the sort of man who, in normal times, the police would have arrested, but when the war started, he made a reputation for himself as a fighter in what he called a special unit of the military police. He was physically very big, which got him noticed. His head was shaved and his nickname was Celo, which means bald. A year after the war started, he had diversified his operations. He drove round in a convertible with a very young girl, who was sexy in a tarty way, and a couple of body-guards. All his men were armed. I would see him swaggering into bars with his moll, wearing a silver pendant shaped like a boxing glove, peeling off money from a thick wad of German marks to buy packets of Marlboro cigarettes, which he through back over his head without looking, knowing that his boys would be there to catch them." First of all, sir, are the words as recorded here accurate and truthful to what you experienced in Sarajevo in relation to this individual?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you've mentioned earlier that are there are several Celos. Is this the Celo that you had just been talking about in reference to the questions posed by the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, indeed. And in reference to what Your Honour said, he was somebody who had a small following. He'd hang out in his place with a dozen guys. I mean, it was that level of -- that level of a following at that particular time, a year after the war started. And he was -- by that time, he'd gone away from being the fighter that he'd been at the beginning and he was much more into racketeering by that point. And so he would sit a bit like -- if you imagine the TV show "The Sopranos," he would sit with his henchmen in the room and you'd go and see the guy, and sometimes you would see him swaggering about town as I described there. But he wasn't -- by that point he was a -- he wasn't a military force. He was a criminal. But he became prominent through fighting at the beginning of the war when he was in this so-called special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that's what I was going to ask you about. So it was your understanding it was a special unit of the military police of the Armija of Bosnia-Herzegovina loyal to President Izetbegovic's side?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, there were all kinds of units and they generally called them -- very often called themselves "special forces" or "special units," with no particular basis in terms of military training. I think they'd just thought it sounded better. It was, as I said, that time in 1992 when they were organising the defence of their part of the city, it was pretty chaotic. And when I was first introduced to this man Celo, he were -- he described himself as being in a special unit and he had a uniform and he was carrying a Kalashnikov, and he said he was a fighter and he was in this special unit, as he called it, of the police -- of the military police. And then I went to find him again a year after the war started, which was when I went to him to this cafe. I saw him swaggering around and he was very much then the mafiosi mobster kind of guy, rather than someone who was -- at this point he wasn't even claiming, I think, to be a fighter. He was into business, criminal business.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we are at the time for the second break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would have a small question in relation to your last answer. You're talking about so-called units and everything being pretty chaotic. When they said that they were special units, did you gain the impression that these units were formed by any higher authority or that they were just self-proclaimed units claiming police powers which may not have or may have formally made available to them? I mean, is it just all self-invented police or was it anywhere in a kind of structure linked to government power and police power?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was my impression, Your Honour, at the beginning of the war - and I'm talking about July 1992 when I first went there - that while there were official units linked to the -- the government, there were also these rather maverick units of which he was one, which I would say they were more self-proclaimed than appointed. They probably had some backing because they were useful. They were doing their -- their job, but I don't think that they took orders from anyone particularly, except for themselves. By the following year, by 1993, there was a man called General Delic who was in charge of the army then, and by then they had a formal headquarters. There were procedures. For example, when I went to Mostar, I had to get various permissions to cross various front lines, and we were able to go to General Delic and ask formally for special letters and accreditation which they were able to grant us. Back in 1992, I -- there wasn't really a procedure like that. So they were starting to organise themselves, but in -- in 1992 it -- I think the best way I would say was quite chaotic, and self-proclaimed units rather than units which were formally invested with powers by -- what was described as the central government but, in fact, was essentially at that point in 1992 a group of leaders who were in the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And were they in 1993, as you described when it was all better organised, were these same people or same units or quasi-units, were they still functioning within that new system, if I could say so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, by then Juka had been forced out, I think, of Sarajevo, and he was later -- as I said in the book, in 1994 he was found dead in Belgium. This original Celo, I don't know what happened to him. Well, he -- by 1993 he was involved in racketeering, not in fighting. So I think that they -- they got their act together actually pretty fast, because they had to, and they were -- I think once former officers of the JNA were involved in it in a more real way, then they were organising themselves more along military lines. And the ragtag of various kinds of Territorial Defence units and people who picked up guns and self-proclaimed special units and so on were slowly regularised into what became, by the end of the war, a much more effective armed force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We -- Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the purposes of scheduling, it would be helpful to know whether it's likely we'll get to the next witness today or whether it will be on Monday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could you in any way assist Mr. Jeremy?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm still on track to complete the witness within the time-period that we had estimated for him, which was three and a half hours. So I would think that I should -- I'm confident that we will take up the remainder of the day with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means the next witness doesn't have to remain standby.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, would you please follow the usher. We'll take a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Just in the interests of trying to ensure the witness is finished today, at the moment I don't have any redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, it's to some extent in your hands whether the witness can leave today. Would you please consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honours, and I'll try my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, I use the opportunity to -- to give you -- yes, I'll do that after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, while -- when we left off, we were talking about these men who had their own units which you described as self-proclaimed, and we had discussed three of them. Earlier, you had mentioned that there was more than one Celo. We have already talked about one who was the mobster. Am I correct that the other Celo was a gentleman by the name of Ramiz Delalic, who, in fact, was the commander of the 9th Mountain Brigade of the Army of BiH?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason why I was a bit vague about that Celo is because I didn't have very much contact with him myself or much knowledge of him. I think I remember towards the end of the war he was quite badly wounded, but apart from that, I don't really have any knowledge of what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. The -- these men and their units whom you've described as being minority players in Sarajevo, is it correct that they would be stationed in and operate outside of school buildings within Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they did, I was not aware of that. I certainly saw no evidence of them operating from or alongside school buildings, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have knowledge that these men, or at least some of them, for instance, Caco with the 10th Mountain Brigade, and the second Celo with the 9th Mountain Brigade, had control over artillery, tanks, mortars, and the like?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't -- I wasn't aware of the kind of armament that they had. The soldiers of -- fighters of Caco who I saw were armed with Kalashnikovs in the main.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. While we still have your book up on the screen, I'd like to look at page 14 of the same in e-court. And once we get there, I'd like to focus on the top of page 151 on the right. You say here, sir: "Reporters should never forget the cruelty of war, but they should also state clearly when crimes are being committed, and if they can, say who is responsible. We should have been harder on the leaders of the Bosnian Serbs who were treated by Western governments and their military representatives, until almost the very end, as legitimate people with whom business could be done." Sir, is this a position that you still adhere to?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was referring to then was that I was very struck by the way that even though there were already serious questions about human rights violations, violations of the laws of war and so on, violations of international humanitarian law that we -- that were being directed especially at the Bosnian Serb leadership, that I'd say -- I'd see UNPROFOR leaders, Western military people, meeting with them, sometimes engaging in a cheery toast, and I just saw a contrast in -- with that behaviour with information that was coming out of -- out of other sources. I felt that -- yeah, I felt that in my own reporting I should have got more into the political context. I concentrated my reporting much more on the -- the plight of civilians rather than going more deeply, as I would now as a more experienced reporter, into the political background of what was happening and the degree to which it seemed to me, at the time, that there was a -- an organised push going on by the Bosnian Serb leadership, for example, in the field of ethnic cleansing. And at the time, I think I mistakenly in my reporting felt that getting into the politics was possibly a little complicated for some of our audience, which I think was a mistake. And if I look back at my reporting of the Bosnian war, that's the thing which I would change. We did an awful lot of the humanitarian side, on the impact of the war on civilians, without going enough into the -- the political reasons why it was happening, and I think that's something which we should have done, and that's what I was referring to there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could now focus on page 24 of the document in e-court, which should correlate to pages 168 and 169. And if we could focus on 169 at the bottom. "Journalists' motives are never pure in these matters either. We also intervene in people's lives, telling ourselves that the upshot of it all will be positive. What right had I to play God when I decided to use my platform on BBC News to make sure that Eldar Kalamujic, the boy with liver failure, was evacuated? The answer is that I thought I was doing good, that I was righting a wrong. But actions have consequences." Sir, is this statement a position you still adhere to as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think to give the full context to that paragraph, you possibly should also have read the paragraph on the previous page where I say that for the only time in my life I decided to manipulate a news story to get Eldar and his family evacuated. What had happened was that after the huge world-wide publicity about the case of -- of one particular girl who was very badly wounded, the British government sent over a plane, a hospital plane to evacuate more children. And I felt they were doing that under a feeling of political pressure that they should do something to help things in Bosnia, because they were also under pressure to intervene militarily, which is what they didn't want to do. And I saw that there was a doctor who went round, and he said -- he went round the hospital, and he said that this particular child wouldn't be evacuated because children in Britain were -- also died of liver failure. And I felt -- because he wasn't wounded. He was just dying of liver failure because his liver was failing. And I felt that was unfair, and I said in the book, and as the UNHCR said, actually -- UNHCR, I quote them as saying: When you come to Sarajevo to evacuate wounded and sick children, you shouldn't pick and choose. So I decided - and I revealed it in that book because it's the only time in my life I've done it - and I decided that why not use the power of the press to embarrass them to evacuate the child as well. So that's what I did. And what I go on to say is that he -- by the time he'd had his liver transplant in London, he had have -- he'd developed brain damage. And while he lived for a few years, and his parents were very delighted that he lived for the few years, and I've spoken to them and they told that they felt I did the right thing, he still lived with brain damage for a few years, and his parents, as I say, feel that we did the right thing in that case. But I felt since this book was about some of the motivations of journalists in covering wars, I felt it was -- in the interests of telling the truth, it was good to get into this particular incident. I was not referring to the way I report other stories. This was one very specific incident as I make very clear on page 168 in the second paragraph down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to focus on an incident you describe in your statement. So if we could have P2515 MFI in e-court, page 11 in English and page 14 in the B/C/S. And it's described at paragraphs 37 and 38 of the same and is the incident with the orphan bus and the shelling of the subsequent funeral. Are you sure this is not another incident where you felt you had to intervene to right a wrong?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely certain, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to look at a few things from that incident with you. First of all, is it correct that one of the orphans killed, Vedrana Glavas, was actually an ethnic Serb, and her family had never given permission for nor knew that she was being taken out of Sarajevo on the convoy?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I never asked the family what their ethnicity was, funnily enough. I was focused on the death of the child. But as I made very clear in my report of that, the family didn't know that she was being taken out and she had been presented by the local aid organisation who fixed up this bungled evacuation, she had -- we were told initially that she was an orphan, and then we found out that she wasn't an orphan. She had a mother and a grandmother. But as for her ethnicity, I didn't actually ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now at paragraph 37 of your statement, you say that they, the bus, were shot at by bullets that appeared to come from Serb positions. You did not have occasion to eyewitness the incoming shots; that is to say, you were not an eye-witness. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of incoming shots, no, I wasn't. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that your initial broadcast report on this incident, as you indicated in direct, according to you, misidentified the location of the bus at the time that it was attacked? The place were the shooters were?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. As I said in my clarification at the beginning of my testimony, I misidentified in that particular part of the report where the shooters were. But actually looking at the video, it's illogical, knowing the geography of Sarajevo better, as I did very shortly afterwards, to say that it could have come from there because that was always in government hands. And we, in the piece, very clearly show a picture of the bus leaving the final Bosnian check-point and driving down the road to Ilidza, which is -- that final Bosnian check-point was probably a good half-mile past the Oslobodjenje building, maybe a little further than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What's the range of a sniper rifle, sir?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends what weapon is used and it depends on the prevailing conditions. It depends on the weather. It depends on the skill of the shooter. It depends on the amount of wind. I think in the hands of a proper sniper rifle, a special sniper rifle with a big calibre bullet, which I don't think was used on this occasion, judging by the wounds that I was told about and saw on the children, has a -- can be, I think, the best part of a kilometre, I am told. I think a Kalashnikov, as I understand it, in the hands of a -- you know, of an accomplished marksman, might be more like 3- or 400 metres. But I'm -- as you pointed out, I am not a military man so I can easily be -- stand corrected on those particular ranges. What I do know is that the shooting incident happened a few minutes after the bus had left the final Bosnian check-point and was heading towards Ilidza, and there was very little space, very little road, because I had driven along the road to Ilidza myself. There was -- there is not a long distance between that. It's a few minutes drive, probably. Four, five minutes, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that your cameraman who had filmed the bus before it left was at the scene immediately after the shootings?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't immediately after the shootings, I believe, because he thought that the bus had gone. They saw the bus leaving. They filmed on the bus as it went towards the final check-point, which is where you saw the pictures of the children tied to the seats with bedsheets. They then left the bus. They took shots of the bus driving off towards Ilidza and then returned to our offices. They -- they didn't -- so they weren't there when -- then we later subsequently heard, I think, an hour or so later about what had happened, and we went back. And I think I'm right in saying -- yeah, by the time we went back, the children were in a makeshift morgue, which wasn't far from the Bosnian check-point. And as you saw in the piece that was actually broadcast in this court yesterday, we had pictures of the two children with sheets over them, and the sheets were bloody. In other words, it wasn't long after they were killed. The blood hadn't congealed. The blood was still flowing out of their bodies when they were put in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that your cameraman received the initial information that the source of fire had been the Oslobodjenje building?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think the cameraman did receive the -- I can't remember where that extraneous report came from. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I again invite you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, be slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to take a break between question and answer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and to be slower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall where that extraneous report came from, but my guess is that it wouldn't have come from any of our local staff because they would have corrected me very quickly as to the -- as to who controlled the Oslobodjenje building at that particular time and throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So was the exclusion of the Oslobodjenje building as a source of fire based upon its location or who controlled it?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was based on its location and who controlled it because the way we worked it out through talking to people who were around the check-point, to talking subsequently as well to UN people, was that their information was that the -- you know, we went to the UNPROFOR people and asked them what their information was, because, of course, there were UNPROFOR soldiers in different places and the information would filter back to their press people. We were told very clearly that the shooting incident took place significantly after the bus had left the final Bosnian check-point. And since -- since you mention it, since the Oslobodjenje building was maybe half a mile back from there, I don't think it's physically possibly for someone to have opened fire from there and to have hit the bus. And my recollection of the pictures of the bus as well were that it would be -- that it was hit from the side. So it wouldn't have been from way back down the road; it would have been from somewhere along the side as it -- after it had left the final Bosnian check-point and as it approached Ilidza. I don't know which point on the road that it -- that it occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to your conclusion of who was responsible for the shooting upon the bus, did you later do any follow-up to determine if any formal investigation of the incident had determined that identity?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so. Things were moving very fast at that particular time. I think we got caught up in other news stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could take a look at something from the Karadzic trial. 1D1349. Page 99 of the same, which ought to correlate to page 10166 of the underlying transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at line 16 and onwards you were asked as follows, sir: "Q. How did you establish that it was the Serbs who shot at the bus? How did you come to reject the theory that that could have been done by Muslim soldiers or, rather, the government, although the theory was supported by the UN? "A. At that point, I hadn't heard the theory that the Bosnian government side were doing it to their own people. I first heard the theory from a military aide to General Lewis MacKenzie, who was the UNPROFOR Sarajevo Sector commander at the time, towards the end of that first visit I paid to Sarajevo, which was August of 1992. So he took me to one side and said, Look, by the way, I want you to know we're convinced that the Serbs -- sorry, that the Bosnian government are shelling themselves. So I said, Well, what evidence have you got? And he said, We don't really have any evidence, but that's what we think." First of all, sir, is this the -- is this the same aide that you are referencing in your statement at paragraph 39, which is at page 12 in the English, page 16 in the B/C/S? Again, that being P2515 marked for identification. Are we talking about the same individual?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, we are talking about the same individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And my first question for you on this topic: Could you identify for us this aide to General MacKenzie that provided this information to you? If you'd like, we can go into private session to do so.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as a journalist I can't reveal my sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Apart from this aide to General MacKenzie, was he the only one that told you of such a conspiracy story or did other UN officials at the time voice or talk about such a thing?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the only UN official who mentioned it. He was -- and he took me aside and told me in an undertone as if it was something that was semisecret. As I said, in the -- as you just were pointing out, I mean, my view was that evidence would have emerged. I think it's -- my experience as a journalist tells me it's very hard to keep things secret for 20 years. I am very surprised that someone hasn't come forward and said, Yes, we did it, if that was indeed the case. As for that bus, it was shot at at quite close range going through Serb-controlled territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it your belief, sir, that there has not been any evidence that has come forth in the intervening 20 years of any single incident of the ABiH side shooting at their own side, for whatever reason?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was in Sarajevo, I saw none of this evidence. Now in the last 20 years, I am aware that there have been some reports, I think, made public, and I've certainly had military figures, military sources sharing information of that nature with me more recently about -- about incidents in 1995. The incident that -- I've heard an assertion that the incident, the attack on the market that prompted NATO intervention, ultimately, in 1995, that there was some evidence that was claimed from crater analysis that the shots had come from the -- the explosions, the mortars had come from the Bosnian side. But as a journal -- I mean, I want to put very much on record that as a journalist, I would have been absolutely delighted to do that story. I would have got a lot of kudos for it and I would have had no hesitation in doing the story. And we tried to look into it as much as we could, about who was shelling whom, and I can absolutely state unequivocally that had I been able to find out that the Bosnian government was shelling their own people and causing a large number of people and causing large numbers of casualties or any casualties, I would have reported it. I absolutely would have. And I never saw that proof. And I haven't seen people coming forward since then and saying, Yeah, you know, we were running an operation that did that. Similar things have -- other kinds of dirty tricks have come out of other conflicts. But not as far as I am aware - and I don't cover the Balkans anymore so I can't pretend to be up to date - but as far as I'm aware, over the subsequent 20 years, I don't think that levels of detail that would support it have come out. I could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So have you not heard of the so-called Seva unit that operated in Sarajevo and conducted such operations?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to look at a document with you. 1D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could I try to clarify at least one thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness said something about shelling their own side. Your next question was about shooting. Did you intend to refer to shelling as well? Because the witness then answered again in terms of shelling. You used a different word. Now I am just trying to find out for myself whether you either misspoke or that you intended to shift from shelling to shooting, and then we could verify with the witness whether his answer would be accurate for shooting as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I originally had asked about shelling and shooting in a general sense for which the witness had said he -- gave his answer, and then I asked specifically about the Seva unit in relation to shooting which -- as opposed to shelling. So it was meant to be a question as to a particular formation for which I believe there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- information that they were shooting, not shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then try to reconstruct what I think happened. The witness told us about someone who had told him that the government forces were shelling their own side. And the witness said, "I'm not going to reveal my sources." He told us that it was the only one who told him about this conspiracy story. It was about shelling. Then you asked him, "Is it your belief," when the witness said that he never had received any evidence on that, "Is it your belief, sir, that there has not been any evidence coming forth in the intervening 20 years of any single of the ABiH side shooting at their own side for whatever reason?" So there we shifted from shelling to shooting. The witness answered that question about 20 years of evidence, focusing on shelling again. And then you asked about the Seva unit, where you refer to Seva unit as "that operated in Sarajevo and conducted such operations," not making it clear whether it was about shelling or shooting. I just want to avoid that there is any misunderstanding. Did you ever receive any evidence about shooting, that is, not shelling but shots being fired at -- within your own territory, your own controlled territory by ABiH forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Subsequently, and I quoted it and it's already been mentioned, I think, this morning, there were stories of some of Caco's people shooting Serbs who were in Bosnian government-held territory. And I think the case -- the accusation against them was that they were summarily executed. I was referring in my answers, and my understanding of that question, actually, about the Seva unit, was that the reference was to shelling, that's what I was mentally focused on. But I -- so all my answers were -- were referring, really, to shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just want --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to avoid any confusion, and that's the reason why I asked him whether you heard about shooting --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. And I have not heard of Seva at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can have 1D1338 in e-court. I think will we see when the document comes up that it is dated the 27th of October, 1994. And it is from UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo to General Rose.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all, looking at this date, were you still covering Bosnia-Herzegovina and Sarajevo at that time?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1994. I'm -- I wasn't in Sarajevo, though, at that particular time. I think that was more or less the time that I was doing that documentary which included the interview with the gentleman, the Serb official, who was engaged in the deportations. So I was more in Bosnian Serb territory at that time. I wasn't -- in the autumn of 1994, I wasn't in the Sector Sarajevo -- in Sarajevo itself as controlled by the BH government.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the Brigadier Fikret that is mentioned in relation to the recce of Igman in this memo?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name rings a bell. He's not someone I met, someone I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me see if I can refresh your recollection. Several witnesses in this trial have identified a Brigadier Fikret, saying he was involved in criminal activities and in charge of smuggle and all traffic through the Butmir airport tunnel. For instance, we had David Fraser at transcript page 5825 through 5826, and RM163 at transcript pages 6164 through 6165. Does that refresh your recollection of a Brigadier Fikret operating in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never really did the story of the tunnel very much. That was done, I think, by colleagues of mine. You know, we took turn and turnabout to go into -- different rotations going into Sarajevo. And I -- I don't recall interviewing Brigadier Fikret, and I certainly never went through the tunnel. I knew -- I knew of its existence, as everybody did, but I didn't report on it myself. I think that would have been done by other BBC people.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You say you knew the tunnel as everyone did. Was it a well-known fact that the tunnel existed and was used for transportation of goods and people in and out of the city?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, well, if I knew about it, I think it was a fair bet that other people knew about it too, yes. I think it was pretty well known. The first reports of it, I can't remember quite where they were, were -- it wasn't quite so believed, but then it became clear that it was happening, and I spoke to people, foreign dignitaries who had been through the tunnel and who told -- described it to me in great detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you think it would be fair to have to take into account the operation of the tunnel, whether by Brigadier Fikret or by some other individual, in terms of evaluating the statements and the responsibility of -- that you attribute to the Serbs for being the ones controlling who was able to get in and out of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tunnel was a hole in the wall. It wasn't a breach of the wall. By "wall," of course, I'm speaking metaphorically. The siege continued. And I think that when people aren't able to move of their own volition easily and safely without being fired on, in that particular case it was a siege. So, yes, there were -- at times the siege was porous. It was porus because of black market activities and corruption and local alliances between people on either side of the front line, and the tunnel was a major hole in it. But in terms of how that affected the condition of the people, the people couldn't go in and out of the tunnel as they wanted. They couldn't go across and visit their families on the other side of the -- of the airport in Butmir through the tunnel. It was very much controlled by the military and used for, I imagine, the transportation of military supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to the second page of this document. At the top we have an item marked "tram, flag B." And it says: "At 1735 hours, 25 October, tram shot area BRATSVA Br, and reported 8 injured. BAT 4 conducts investigation (see report) "Conclusions "- sentries and police suggest rounds near north bank of river. "- paint chips suggest tram located NE of police Kiosk. "- trajectory of rounds suggest shooter near ground level and from BiH side of river. "- all evidence and corroboration by Bosnian officials indicate shots came from Bosnian-held territory (see map for building)." Did you, I suppose, not have knowledge of this incident around the 25th of October, 1994, at the Bratsva, I think, bridge, where a tram was shot at and eight persons were injured?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as I say, I wasn't in the city at that particular time. I mean, if as a journalist I had seen this particular document at the time, it would have been a great story, and I would have -- I would probably have asked why was it also corroborated by Bosnian officials? I mean, that's my journalistic response to it. But no, I wasn't -- that's hypothetical because I wasn't in the city at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you think -- do you think had you had access to information about an incident like this one would have made you rethink or retract your assessment of the validity or not of the conspiracy theory that we had talked about from paragraph 39 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not retract. Because I was thinking more there about major shelling operations against people inflicting mass casualties. I think it would have been a -- as I say, it would have been a story that would have been, you know, this -- that would have been a -- if they had made that public at the time, maybe they did, but had it been made public at the time, it would have been a significant story, certainly. Yeah, it would have been. But, you know, I think with all these things, you have to take them -- take the individual circumstances of each particular incident. And going back to that incident with the bus, seeing this doesn't make my change my mind about conclusions I drew at the time because of the location of the bus where it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand that. I was asking about the --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- observations you made about the conspiracy theory in paragraph 39 of the statement. Just so we're clear.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that one incident necessarily confirms the whole theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would move to admit this document into evidence as the next available Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wouldn't oppose admission on the basis of context. It's been discussed today. Although, you know, I would note that the witness wasn't in Sarajevo at the time of this incident. And I'd also note that so far as I'm aware, this document wasn't put to General Rose while he was here as one might expect under Rule 90(E). But I do not oppose admission of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you do not oppose admission. Then we leave it to that. Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1338 receives number D387, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Ivetic, it would certainly assist the Chamber, but I don't know whether it does exist or not, all evidence and corroboration by Bosnian officials indicate shots came from Bosnian-held territory. The witness was -- your interest was triggered by this observation that the Bosnian would have corroborated this to be the source of fire. If there is any further material about that, I think it would be interesting for the Chamber to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Understood. I will try to find out if there is anything more. I don't have anything at this time. Otherwise I would have brought it to Your Honours' attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can please have 1D1336 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And as you can see, it is dated the 17th of August, 1994, and it's from the UN Centre for Human Rights Field Office in Sarajevo in relation to a meeting with General Soubirou of UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo. Now, I'd like to have a look at the second page of the same and focus in on item number 2 at the second half of the page. "The BiH government seemed to present the International Community with propaganda regarding violations committed by the Serb side, omitting to do the same regarding violations committed by them. "For example, the civilian population has major administrative obstacles in leaving Sarajevo, and the police and military officials, being powerful, contribute significantly to this policy." The question I first have for you, sir: Did you ever have access to any information of this type, from international officials or other sources, that the BiH government was imposing administrative obstacles to keep people from leaving Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to clarify, just so I'm clear in my own mind, this is a statement, is it, from -- oh, I touched the screen. I beg your pardon. From the general, from General Soubirou?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we'll see its from the field office --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- of the UN Centre for Human Rights to the chief of Special Procedures branch of the United Nations Centre for Human Rights in Geneva, talking about a meeting that they had with General Soubirou, is the way I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, yeah, okay. So the question was, was I aware of these administrative hurdles that were put in place by the BiH government and the army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct. That prevented people from leaving Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear as time went on in the war -- I did hear as time went on in the war that there were those kinds of hurdles put on the -- put in the -- as obstacles for some people to leave, and I wondered at the time did that change the status of the situation there as a siege. I felt it did not because my understanding of that was that they were trying to keep people there as part of their war effort and that the -- the thing that had set it all off in the first place was the imposition of the siege. And also my understanding, too, was that it didn't mean that it was impossible for people to leave Sarajevo because I was aware of quite a lot of people who left Sarajevo at that particular time. But I do think that, you know, it was a -- as they organised themselves more, they became increasingly bureaucratic. And I think you had to have a lot of paperwork to move, to get permissions to travel and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you think that your statement of approximately 21 pages that omits any reference to this that you had knowledge of, that the BiH side was imposing obstacles to people leaving Sarajevo, is really accurate and impartial in assessing that the Bosnian Serbs were the ones that kept people from leaving Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think the -- what's revealed in that document in the opinion of the -- of this UNPROFOR general affects the fundamental fact of the siege really one iota. The siege was imposed and kept going by military force from the Bosnian Serb side, and as a -- as a result of the siege and the way that things continued, life became very corrupt and difficult and unjust for quite a few people inside Sarajevo. It was in no sense a happy place. People didn't live in some harmony of pulling together, necessarily. It was a divided and unhappy place where some people had permission to get in and out and some people didn't. But my opinion that the siege was imposed and prosecuted by the Bosnian Serb side doesn't change as a result of that. I feel that that's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, let's step a way from the opinion of the author of this document and let's talk about what you just testified that you knew about which is not in your statement. Do you believe that the failure to include in your statement which you knew about these obstacles being put in place by the BiH side to keep people from leaving Sarajevo, if you're statement accurately and impartially describes matters, even though it fails to include this information that you just testified you did know about?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That statement isn't an account of everything I knew about the situation in Sarajevo from beginning to end. I was there regularly for -- for three years. I don't think that it -- no, because I think that the -- as I said, I believe that the -- the fact that there were some bureaucratic obstacles that were put in place was troubling for those people that were affected by them. It effect everybody by any means, and I don't think, to repeat, that it gets away from the fact that the siege was imposed by the Bosnian Serbs. I travelled on a regular basis along the roads to Pale, past Bosnian Serb positions, and I saw the guns, I saw the piles of spent shell casings and bullet casings from -- everything from .50-calibre weapons up to anti-aircraft and heavier and tanks as well that were firing into the city. I spoke to the gunners in those places through a translator, once or twice they spoke English, maybe a few times. But I spoke through a translator who -- and these men cheerfully admitted what they were doing. They let us film down the barrels of their guns that were targeted in places within the city. That's a siege. I'm sorry, it is. And that was the fundamental fact in the reason why there had to be an air-lift to bring in -- why there had to be an air-lift, to bring in relief supplies, because there was a siege. What were those men doing on the hills, who, as I say, I very regularly saw and spoke to and saw the piles of spent shell casings. What were they doing other than prosecuting a siege? And I think that if the exit of some people as a result of bureaucratic problems -- it's not like they were stopped at the barrel of a gun from doing it. It was because they didn't have the correct forms. I don't think that's comparable and I don't think it dilutes the fact that a siege was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were Caco's men in the 10th Mountain Brigade stopping people at the barrel of a gun from leaving the territory?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've absolutely no idea what they were doing, because they certainly weren't operational. Their zone of operation was nowhere near the tunnel that went to Butmir and nowhere near the -- those particular -- that end of the city. It was more near the old city, and looking up at those heights towards the -- the bobsleigh run. So that was their -- their main centre of operations. They had a little enclave there at the height of his powers. It was very strongly -- I know this because when I travelled to Mostar in -- first of all in August of 1993, to cross the -- the runway through various check-points controlled by the BiH Army, I had to get an official permission from the -- the office, the military headquarters of General Delic who, at that point, was the military commander, and the people who we dealt with on the check-points were uniformed members of the BiH forces. So they weren't -- that was still the Caco era, I believe, and so no, they couldn't have been in contact -- in touch in -- in control of that particular place at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I please have leave to consult with my client briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may if Mr. Mladic will keep his -- the volume of his voice down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, Mr. Ivetic, would it assist if we take the break a little bit earlier so that you have more time to consult? We are close to the point where we would take --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That would, Your Honours, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll take the break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I meanwhile use the time for the following. On the 1st of October of this year, the Prosecution tendered 65 ter 28036, which was initially tendered through Witness RM506, and the Defence indicated that they needed to consider whether they have any objections to admission. They were instructed to do so not later than that week, transcript page 17711, and the Defence is invited to clarify their position in relation to this. Not necessarily immediately, unless it could be a simple yes or no, but at least as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we still have the document on the screen, I'd like to look at item number 4 on the list as it relates to Rogatica, which is also a topic that you covered in the witness statement at paragraph 10, for instance. This document reads: "Concerning the forced eviction of civilians in Rogatica which was covered by the media as ethnic cleansing, General Soubirou believes that it was part of an agreement between the two parties." Did your inquiries as a journalist uncover any information tending to point to the fact that population exchanges in Rogatica in 1994 in the month of August were, in fact, negotiated between the two parties?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never saw any evidence of that. But then again, I didn't look for it. As I say again, I wasn't in the city at that particular time. My references to Rogatica earlier on were, I think, in connection with incidents that happened there in 1992, 1993. Certainly people there spoke to me about the situation in Rogatica as I was passing through it on my way to Gorazde in 1992, and I subsequently spoke to people who had been displaced from Rogatica to Sarajevo when they were in Sarajevo, and I remember them telling me about particularly brutal treatment, including rapes, at the hands of Serb forces there. Whether or not that was by agreement, I have absolutely no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I now propose to take a look at a short video-clip of less than one minute. It is one for which the transcript has not been verified, so I will first play it once through and then play it a second time in accord with the procedure Your Honours have identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The transcripts were distributed to the booths yesterday -- or I should say the transcript, I only have it in one language, English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. The number is 1D1354.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed as you suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Playing it the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I note I'm not getting sound.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, me neither.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps while we try to get that sorted, I can go and make use of our time to ask other questions and return to this. If we can call up 1D1337.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it is quite difficult -- now it's disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this document is dated 9 November 1994. It is from the UNPROFOR investigative team led by a Lieutenant-Colonel Le Chevalier of Sector Sarajevo, and indicates that it is a technical report on mortar shells. If we look at the description of the incident, in the middle of the page it indicates that two 82-millimetre mortar shells landed at Livanjska Street. First of all, sir, would you agree with me that this location at Livanjska Street would be within BiH-controlled territory as confirmed by the fact that the presence of the Bosnian police were at the scene of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to take your word for that because I don't remember specifically a street of that name or its location.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 3 in both the B/C/S and the English, I'd like to focus on the conclusion reached by this UN team. "Conclusion: "It is possible to conclude that the most suspected area are under the control of BiH. "To fire from BSA positions for the same ranges and with the same angle of descent, the direction of the mortar should be 4200 milliems (from Grdonj) or 700 milliems (from Orlovac) which means that the direction of the weapon measured from the impact location should be 1000 milliems (Grdonj) or 700 milliems (Orlovac). The impacts on the ground are too clear to allow such errors. To fire from BSA positions and from the direction between 1200 and 1600 milliems, the distance should be at least 3700 metres. The angle of descent in that case should be less than 60 degrees." Would you agree, sir, that this is pretty convincing evidence that the BiH side fired the mortar shells in question?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say I've never heard the word "milliem" before. I don't quite know what it means. But going from the first sentence in that conclusion, it's possible to conclude the most suspected are under the control of BiH, I assume from that that they're saying that the greater likelihood was that the mortars were fired from their positions. I wasn't in the city at the time. I can't comment on the specific incident. As a journalist and as an observer, what I would say -- my first question would be: Well, what was the intent of the attack if it did come from the BiH area? Were they are targeting something? Were they trying to hit Bosnian Serb positions and it dropped short? Was it a misfire? You know, it raises as many questions as it answers in my mind. And as for the technical information about angles of descent and milliems, I -- I mean I am not an expert about that. I have no knowledge of it so I can't comment, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. At this trial, David Fraser, who was the MA to the Sector Sarajevo chief of UNPROFOR in 1994 and 1995, testified at transcript page 5880 through 5882 about his knowledge of several incidents of attempted deception by the ABiH side, including one where the site of a shell that came from the Serb side was subsequently shelled by the BiH side when people came out to investigate the first shell, both causing casualties. In that instance, a joint BiH and UN investigation confirmed that whereas the first shell came from the Serb side, the second shell was confirmed to have come from the BiH side. Can we conclude that you did not have knowledge of such incidents as reported by -- by General Fraser, who at that time was a major?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- no, I didn't have knowledge of that incident. Not at all. They weren't, I think, in the habit of sharing that kind of thing with the press in -- openly anyway. And so no, I didn't have any knowledge of that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would knowledge of incidents like these that we have just gone through cause you to reconsider your conclusions in paragraph 39 of your statement about the "conspiracy theory" within the UN?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I mean, I see questions as well as answers in that assertion from General, then Major, Fraser. For example, I'm again intrigued by the Bosnian authorities who were involved in the investigation and also seemingly corroborating it. I think perhaps they were implying that there were freelance operators who were throwing in shells, perhaps. So to make a proper comment on that, really, I feel I would need the full context and the full story, rather than just a couple of lines taken by themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to look at another part of your Rule 92 ter statement. P2515 MFI, page 8 in the English, page 11 of the B/C/S. Paragraph 25 of the same. Here you talk of the time you spent at both the Kosevo and state hospitals in Sarajevo, and you talk of holes from tank rounds in the walls of the state hospital. First of all, did Kosevo Hospital appear to have similar damage and tank-round holes when you visited that hospital?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was in a different kind of location. The state hospital is a -- quite a high building which -- it's multiple floors. I think it's probably eight -- six or eight floors, perhaps, and it directly faces the positions on the -- on the mountain which the Serbs were in control of, and there was a direct line of fire from those positions into the -- the state hospital, which meant that those upper floors, which I went up to and examined myself, and again this was early in the war, those upper floors were uninhabitable. They had large holes in the windows big enough for a human being to fall out, and they were -- everybody had been moved down into the basement. The Kosevo Hospital was -- it's a -- it's more of a low-rise building, which was damaged, but it's more sprawling, it's more spread out, and in a somewhat different position strategically to -- geographically, I should say, to the state hospital. It was right in the -- much more in the centre of town. Kosevo is a bit more off to the edge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, before I forget, you put the evidence of Mr. Fraser to the -- to the witness. I think when that evidence was given, I addressed both Prosecution and Defence, Ms. Bolton and you, to see whether there was any further documentation, any contemporaneous reports about that. Have you consulted with the Prosecution on that matter and what is the result of this strong invitation to provide the Chamber with a detailed report so that we are better able to access the -- the value of the evidence in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that we found any documents in relation to that. My recollection was at that time when we consulted with the Prosecution that they were unaware of any documents. I don't remember offhand whether there was a date mentioned by General Fraser. I believe it was without an actual date for the incident, which would make it hard to locate documents. Although, we will obviously look. But as I stand up on my feet, I do not remember being able to find any written reports or other -- other written material about this incident apart from the reference in the one statement by General Fraser, his testimony in, I believe, one other proceeding, and a reference to the same incident in a prior statement dating closer to the time-period of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I hear from the Prosecution as well, whether Ms. Bolton was any -- successful and whether she sat together with Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd have to take some time to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: -- inquire about and come back to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber is very much interested in detailed evidence if these important matters are the subject matter of evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you, in the course of your work, ever have occasion to hear about a Colonel John Hamill, an Irish officer within, first, the UNMOs and, later, a UN artillery expert brought in to investigate the first so-called Markale market shelling?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never met that gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Hamill was a witness for the Prosecution at this trial, and he talked about some damage he found at Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can call that up, it's 1D1352 in e-court. Page 2 of the same, which is the print-out of transcript page 5514 of our trial transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to go through some of this with you to see if this relates to anything that you would have seen. Let's start -- well: "Q. Starting with the question, and it will tell you the time-frame I'm talking about, sir: "'Q. On the 5th of December, 1993, you went to Kiseljak to attend a conference, and then you moved to the Papa side. You saw the Kosevo Hospital, and you saw the two nurses and one doctor killed by a shell. You also saw a hole in a wall over 1 metre in diameter, forming almost a perfect circle. Do you remember that? "'A. That is almost correct. I didn't see any nurses or a doctor killed. I was informed when we were there that there had been those casualties when the building was hit by a shell, but that had happened some time before and I don't know when. I did see the hole in the wall. It was a large one, and it was almost a perfect circle. So, yes, that part is correct.' "First of all, when you're talking -- does this comport with your recollection, your factual observations at the Kosevo Hospital building in December of 1993? "A. Yes, my answer does. The question obviously doesn't. "Q. And am I correct that you reached a conclusion based upon this factual observation as to the fire more likely having come from inside the Muslim or Papa zone, rather than from the VRS, as is, I believe, contained in the next four lines of the transcript? "A. That was my opinion, yes." Sir, did you have such information that, in fact, damage to the Kosevo Hospital had been the result of tank round damage that probably came from the BiH side as Mr. Hamill indicates in this portion of the transcript that I've discussed with you?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he never shared his opinion with me, I never met him, and so I didn't know have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have occasion to see the hole that he's talking about at Kosevo Hospital during any of your trips to the same?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember an almost perfect circle in the wall. No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we are on the topic of the hospitals, several witnesses at this trial have talked about mobile ABiH mortars mounted on vehicles, firing rounds from near or at the hospital to attract return fire from the Serbs. For instance, we have had Pyers Tucker, at transcript page 3847, in relation to Kosevo Hospital; General Abdel-Razek, at transcript page 3639, talking about the use of such mortars at humanitarian buildings; John Jordan, at transcript page 1818 to 1820, talking about Kosevo Hospital; Francis Roy Thomas, at transcript page 5172, talking about Kosevo Hospital; and Colonel Richard Mole, at transcript page 4412 through 413, talking about Kosevo Hospital. Sir, did you have any such information about mobile mortars deployed and fired by the BiH side from near hospitals or humanitarian buildings to draw the fire of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have that information. I knew that in the area where we were in Sarajevo, where I was sleeping at the Holiday Inn hotel and where we had an office as well, that there was outgoing fire that would come sometimes very loudly from near there. I know that they sometimes had a recoilless rifle that they used near there. And I did hear outgoing fire coming from the region -- I mean, from that -- the area around the hotel at times. I didn't have any information. I wasn't ever told any information about such a thing happening from near the hospital, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Again, I ask you now, having in mind these additional -- this additional information, the testimony of Colonel Hamill, these instances of the ABiH using -- deploying mobile mortars, would any of that cause you to change your conclusions as to the -- or to revisit the conclusions as to the conspiracy theory of the UN that we talked about earlier from paragraph 39 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think if I'd been privy -- well, I think if I'd been privy to that information at the time, I would have wanted to look into it myself and find out how true it was, what those officers based the information on. I would like also to try and find out -- to speak first-hand to some of the people who were alleged to have done that or perhaps more likely speak to more people who were alleged to -- who said that they'd heard it or seen it, speaking to witnesses about that. It's really very difficult for me based on just a few snippets of information that you give me, to come to a -- you know, a firm and settled conclusion about whether or not that changes what I saw myself in that particular time. One thing I've learned over the years as a journalist is that experts of all sorts are at times fallible as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've not been able to verify the various transcript references that Mr. Ivetic has provided. We have taken a look at one of those references in relation to Witness Tucker, transcript page 3847, and there we don't see anything about the ABiH using mobile mortars to attract return fire from the Serbs. So just a little bit concerned about the characterisation of some of the evidence that we -- we've already heard in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could you -- where there is a challenge to your source, your reference, could you take us to page 3847 so as to indicate where we find --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Your Honour, the transcripts are not in e-court of our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you can -- we all can use the e-court system. So if you tell me on what page, then even without the e-court --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Talking about mobile mortars that were launched from Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 3847, just taking a look. Could you guide me to the -- 3847. I am at that page on my system.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately from the courtroom, we can't use the other LiveNotes. I'm stuck with the scrolling one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, at least on page 3847, reference is made to the shelling conducted from the Kosevo Hospital by a group of Bosnian Muslim mortars. Although it doesn't say anything about them being mobile, but is that what --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, my -- my concern is the suggestion that this was done for the purpose of drawing return fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you just said that nothing was said about mobile mortars. Now, firing from a hospital ground, for whatever reason, whether or not to attract -- I mean, there is a basis for what Mr. Ivetic said, on that page, although perhaps not in exactly the same wordings, isn't it? Page 3847, let me read it aloud, because if it's not. "Yesterday at transcript page," so-and-so, it starts on line 1, "I would like to get more details about the incident where you describe at paragraph 303 of your statement on the same page that we have now, just a little lower. The shelling conducted from the Kosevo Hospital by a group of Bosnian Muslim mortars." Or is it your position that they had fixed mortar positions there?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No, I accept there is a reference to mobile mortars and perhaps I wasn't clear in my objection. My objection is to the suggestion that these mobile mortars were being used in, for instance, Kosevo Hospital for the purpose of drawing return fire onto the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's not how I understood your observation. But check the other ones and we'll see. Mr. Ivetic, meanwhile you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we can ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Today at temporary transcript at page 16, line 2, I asked you a question and you responded as follows: "Would you agree that a journalist has a professional obligation to investigate and verify facts given by others before reporting the same to ensure that they are accurate?" And your answer was recorded as: "Yes, I would agree up to a point. But sometimes it's necessary to report people's views, not to treat them as statements of fact but to make clear in one's reporting that you're reporting someone's view, someone's perception of a situation. So that doesn't mean that one would conduct a major investigation into, say, a statement made by somebody at a presentation conference or in an interview, particularly if that person was speaking from a position of responsibility. What you'd say is that this is the point of view given by that individual." Sir, do you make clear in your reporting when you are reporting your own view or perception of a situation?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't report my own views. I make professional judgements based on observation, on talking to people, most especially when it came to Sarajevo on what I saw and heard myself. I think to expand on the point that you were making regarding my answer and the quotation you gave from my answer, it's quite clear that everybody who speaks particularly to the media, especially if they are in a position of power or strength, tends to speak to an incident from their own perspective, and that's why it's very important to -- to try and lay out the provenance of those remarks. As a BBC journalist, I don't stand up and say: These are my views. What I do is make professional judgements based on the information that I have at any given time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that you are the subject of a finding by the Editorial Standards Committee of the BBC Trust, that in your report of 4 June 1997, "How 1967 defined the Middle East," that that article had breached the BBC impartiality guidelines?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was 2007, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You are correct. 2007. In relation to this, is it correct that the Editorial Standards Committee found that you had not clearly indicated that you were presenting a thesis or interpretation on a highly controversial subject and that other views were available?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that we are short of time, but since you've chosen to bring up this particular, quite controversial decision made by the Editorial Standards Committee of the BBC, I'm afraid it might, Your Honour, take a couple of minutes to explain some of the context, and I'll make it as brief as I can. Covering the Middle East, and especially the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, means that my work is pretty much constantly subjected to the criticism and sometimes formalised complaints through the BBC complaints procedure, often by organised, deeply unimpartial -- deeply partial, lobbies. Now, in this particular situation, the -- a paid lobbyist in the United States and a very active lobbyist in Britain got together and, between the two of them, they put together a long, long list of complaints. In the end, I would say that the BBC Editorial Standards Committee made a flawed decision which was incorrect, and I think the -- the substance of that is -- of me saying that is based on the fact that I received no censure from the BBC about it. I received, in fact, from senior BBC people a lot of support. They had a feeling that our complaints process was flawed, and as a result of that, the incorrect decision had been made by people who weren't well informed. There was a particular issue about whether or not I was going to reveal a source. They said that had I revealed the source, then the veracity of what I'd written would be -- would be clearer. Now, obviously a journalist doesn't reveal a source, so I didn't. It so happened that the point that they were making, I had a very good source for it, but I respected that guy's identity and didn't reveal it. So, yes, they did make a finding against me, and I continue to reject their decision and I am comforted in that by the fact that my peers and, most particularly, the management of the company I work for also effectively rejected it by not censuring me in any way for that. I should say that the Editorial Standards Committee is part of the BBC's governing body which is connected to the BBC, the BBC Trust, but not exactly of the BBC. In fact, its status is -- it's a slightly grey area exactly what its status is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
