utterances.text: Is it correct that you were the subject to the finding by the Editorial Standards Committee for the BBC Trust for your 12 January 2008 BBC Radio 4 report "From Our Correspondent" which breached BBC accuracy guidelines?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The accuracy finding was about the -- the source that I was talking about. They said -- it was about the American attitude towards settlements in the occupied territories, and they bizarrely came up with an idea that if I had said -- a senior American official had told me that they treated them -- they treated the area as occupied territory even though in their public statements they didn't condemn settlements at that time under the Bush administration. I was told that had I revealed my source, they could have found it as an accurate -- they would have found it as an accurate statement; but because I didn't reveal my source, it was therefore inaccurate. Now, in any standards of journalism, that's nonsensical. There was mainly a lay panel who didn't understand the way that we worked. So again --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So again, I would say that I agree that they found that. I disagree with their findings. And again, my management also effectively did because, once again, there was no censure at all. In fact, there was only support coming from them. And I should say from that that there was a -- a change in the -- after that particular incident, the BBC started looking at its complaints procedure with a fear that it had been -- there risks it could be hijacked by professional complainants who were able to put together sophisticated lobbying campaigns, and since then it's been changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it accurate that the Editorial Committee of the BBC Trust stated that: "Jeremy Bowen had stated his professional view without qualification or explanation and that the lack of precision in his language rendered the statement inaccurate. The committee considered that the Middle East editor should have either sourced his comment or stated that it was what officials felt privately but couldn't say."

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I'm -- my response to that is covered by what I've already said, that they believed that I should have revealed my source and then magically the statement would become accurate. I mean, I think that's frankly gobbledygook, and, again, was the result of inexperienced people getting under the sway of professional lobbyists.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To read further: "The committee considered that the Middle East editor should have either sourced his comments or stated that it was what officials felt privately but couldn't stated." Couldn't you have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- quote you read out a second ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Isn't that a less severe option, to give that additional information without naming the source if, in fact, you felt you could not reveal your source?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were actually referring to about four words I put into a parenthesis, between two commas. I didn't -- you don't, in every statement that you write, say exactly what the source was for that particular statement because if you did, there would be no kind of coherent flow of argument in a piece. So, no, I felt that the fact that I had it on background from a very senior former US official backing up my -- I wrote that based on something I'd been told by a very senior US official. I was prepared to approach him and if ask his -- if he was okay about his identity being revealed to the Editorial Standards Committee, and they said, No, that won't be necessary. So again, I stand by what I wrote and I feel that they made a serious professional error in doing what they did. And they were widely criticised within the journalistic profession, not just within the BBC, for what they did and by -- what was seen -- widely seen as a flawed judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the BBC Trust has the general function of setting the strategic framework for the BBC in accordance with the Royal Charter and Framework Agreement?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's in their remit. Yeah, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the rulings by the BBC, upholding complaints against journalists, as was seen in your case, is not a regular occurrence at the BBC?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think that they -- they make -- to be honest, I don't follow in any detail at all what the Editorial Standards Committee do, except insofar as it has applied to my work over the years. I just know that I have spoken to senior people within the BBC Trust subsequently, very senior people, who have said -- who have pretty much dismissed what the Editorial Standards Committee said to me at that particular time. The Trust itself has become quiet a controversial body within Britain, and there is talk about it being changed or reformed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how many of your colleagues, senior editors within the BBC have had similar rulings upheld against them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if it was your purpose to draw the attention of the Chamber to two instances where the -- the committee has given a negative verdict on reporting, I do understand the reporting not related to Bosnia-Herzegovina, then you have achieved that goal. Now, of course, we could deal with the statistics on how often it happens. That's -- you have drawn our attention to that. And the witness has been giving an answer. So if you think you would need another minute to do that, I would not stop you, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I would like to know how many of his colleagues have had similar rulings against them or upheld complaints, I should say, against them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest that the parties together provide the Chamber with statistical information about the number of cases brought before the BBC committee, and to give the Chamber detailed information about all that so that we are provided with the evidence, Mr. Ivetic, you think we would need. We'll then have a look at it and we'll decide whether we really need it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No objection to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. The parties are encouraged to undertake this effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we can call up 1D1344 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you still need, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have approximately 15 minutes, I think, including -- we should be able to get the video if it's -- if the audio is not functioning. The video itself is, I believe, only 48 seconds, so twice would be about two minutes, give or take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you have any further questions, Mr. Jeremy?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Not at this point, Your Honours. And I would also say, for the video 1D1354, that's actually -- it looks like the second half of the very first video that I played yesterday. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you mean that there is no need to have it played again unless there are specific questions about the -- what we see?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, the Chamber has considered the -- and we have, of course, looked at how you developed your cross-examination. The Chamber grants you ten minutes. If, at least, we get the support of the booth to continue for -- to go over 12 minutes to the usual time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can have 1D1344 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is from an organisation with a web site known as BBC Watch. And I just want to see if a quote they attribute to you is accurate. If we can turn to page 3. And it's there in the middle of the page. "We all come from somewhere; we all have a prism through which we see the world; we all have an education, and views and experiences. It's a false objective to be objective. "But I think I can be impartial by trying to disentangle all the threads that make up a story. That's an ambitious thing to do in two and a half minutes on TV. You have got to be aware of what your own prejudices and principles are and put them to one side in a box." Do you acknowledge these words as your own from a 2006 interview with, I believe, Ian Burrell?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's probably an accurate quote. I can't remember precisely. One point I would like to make is that BBC Watch is an utterly biassed and partial organisation which exists essentially to discredit the BBC. It's an operation which is highly pro-Israel and it's designed to try to get the BBC to -- to adopt a pro-Israeli narrative at all times. So it is an accurate quote but it's a pretty flawed source. I can explain what I meant in that statement, if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if Mr. Ivetic wants his -- to use his ten minutes in this way, he'll tell you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we can have 1D1342 in court -- in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe this will be an article authored by you relating to the situation in Egypt. If we can turn to the second page in e-court, here you go talking about the Muslim Brotherhood, and you say: "The country's only properly organised mass political movement outside the ruling party is the Muslim Brotherhood, and it would do very well in any free election. "Unlike the jihadis, it does not believe it is at war with the West. It is conservative and nonviolent. But it is highly critical of Western policy in the Middle East." Do you stand by your assessment of the Muslim Brotherhood?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I would like to actually add some context to that. As you all know if you've been following events in Egypt, the Muslim Brotherhood, which actually went on to win a free election, as I've mentioned there, they had a free election and the Muslim Brotherhood won it, and there was a Muslim Brotherhood president who was removed by the army in a military coup. And since then there has been some violence in the country as a result of that, considerable violence, and a lot of people, not least Muslim Brotherhood supporters, have been killed. But what the Muslim Brotherhood still does not have is an official creed of violence. There was a lot of debate within the movement in the 1960s, and the 1950s, about whether they should go back to a policy of violence which they'd had earlier in their history, and because the mainstream leadership of the movement decided against it, other splinter groups, which became jihadi groups, in fact, some that went on to become al-Qaeda, split away from the Muslim Brotherhood and went down that road. The people I was referring to, which is the very conservative - with a small C, and also with a big C, I suppose - leadership of the Brotherhood in Egypt and in other countries, does have no creed of -- of violence. So yes, I would -- with those, with that extra context, I would absolutely stand by what I wrote back then before the fall of Mubarak.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with Mahdi Akef?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mahdi Akef? You'd have to remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up 1D1341.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the Chamber is not assisted at this moment by hearing answers to those questions, unless in one question you can make it perfectly clear what the relevance is. Apparently you are challenging the opinion expressed by the witness when he is reporting on matters, which is not the same as giving testimony on matters. So therefore, will you please keep this in mind for the remaining three minutes you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Looking at the middle of the screen, and this is from up front -- hurryupharry.org, the guide of the Muslim Brotherhood identified as Mahdi Akef is quoted here as stating in response to a question regarding resistance and jihad. "... do you consider Osama Bin Laden a terrorist or an Islamic Mujahid?" And Akef is quoted as saying: "Certainly, a mujahid, and I have no doubt in his sincerity in resisting the occupation, drawing closer to God Almighty." Did your research into the Muslim Brotherhood reveal such sentiments as expressed by Mahdi Akef and as reflected in this document prior to publishing your article that we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have spoken at length to senior members of the Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood, both on camera and on background, and I have heard many condemnations of the actions of Osama Bin Laden, of al-Qaeda, of all those who follow what's known as attack theory idealogy. Frankly, when it comes to the Middle East, you can search the internet and find all kinds of things on fringe blogs and web sites like this hurryupharry.org, which will -- you can -- you can -- build any argument you like based on them. But I have actually spoken to the main players involved, and I can tell you that I have heard a lot of condemnation from them about Osama Bin Laden. And the fact is, among the vast majority of Muslims in the Middle East, the activities of al-Qaeda and Osama Bin Laden are deeply unpopular because his main targets and al-Qaeda's main targets are often Muslims who they accuse of being apostates. So no, I -- for your Middle East information, I suggest you don't go to hurryupharry.org. I don't think it's a particularly good source.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I shouldn't go to BBC Trust either?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go to the BBC web site is what I'd suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But not the BBC Trust --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic, there is one sentence, perhaps I spoke too quickly, which is missing from the transcript. I think that is that the Chamber was not assisted by hearing the answer to the question unless in the next question you could immediately establish the relevance. You failed to do so. Apart from that, I didn't interrupt you, the ten minutes are over. So this concludes your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I play the videotape that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- court technical services did not permit me to play earlier, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Ivetic. I told you that you had ten minutes left and I interrupted you halfway, where I said we were not assisted by what you elicited from this witness. You nevertheless continued. Therefore, my question now to you, Mr. Jeremy, is whether you have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I want it stated on the record that the Defence was not permitted to play a videotape that it had tried to present earlier which the court services would not have audio for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is already on the record, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, you asked whether you could do it, and I said no, you can't because you have spent your last ten minutes in a different way. And the ten minutes were based upon the Chamber's observation on how you conducted your cross-examination. Mr. Bowen, I would like to thank you very much for having come to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Thank you very much, ladies and gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, and I have to ask for the indulgence for another two or three minutes on an urgent matter which I would have certainly postponed if it was not urgent. I briefly deal with the following matter. It is a decision concerning the Prosecution's proposal regarding the Theunens expert report. On the 25th of September, 2013, the Chamber informed the parties of its inclination to deny part 1 of the Theunens report and asked the Prosecution to elicit any relevant matters related to this part during the examination of the witness. On the 27th of September, after further submissions by the Prosecution, the Chamber invited the Prosecution to make a proposal on how to best elicit the most relevant information dealt with in part 1, short of having the whole part admitted into evidence. The Chamber gave as an example that the Prosecution could consider tendering a drastically reduced selection of part 1, perhaps in the area of 10 or 15 per cent of it, which, together with the focused examination of Theunens, could provide the Chamber with the information needed. On the 2nd of October, the Prosecution submitted a proposal to redact approximately 50 pages of the approximately 180-pages long part 1. Having reviewed the unredacted portions, the Chamber's position is still that part 1 is excessive in length in light of its apparent limited relevance. The Chamber would therefore prefer that the Prosecution elicit any relevant matters related to part one during the examination of Mr. Theunens. The Prosecution should inform the Chamber and the Defence in due course about the additional time it needs for this purpose. That is our statement in relation to the testimony of Mr. Theunens. We adjourn for the day and we resume Monday, the 21st of October, 2013, at 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 21st day of October, 2013, at 9.30 a.m. 24 25
